groups.g: Systems - Oil, Fuel, Electrical and Powerplant

items.x: Not an acronym. The term is detonation, also called engine knock.
items.d: Detonation is an uncontrolled, explosive ignition of the fuel-air mixture inside the cylinder's combustion chamber instead of a smooth, progressive burn. The Gold Seal guide lists three causes: using a fuel grade lower than recommended, running high manifold pressure with low RPM, and running high power with an excessively lean mixture. You discuss it whenever the examiner asks what can destroy an engine, and you avoid it with the correct fuel grade, a rich enough mixture, and a lower pitch attitude for better cooling airflow. The Warrior has no cowl flaps, so airspeed and mixture are the pilot's only cooling controls.
items.reg: 14 CFR Part 91, Subpart A, Section 91.9, Civil aircraft flight manual, marking, and placard requirements; Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, FAA-H-8083-25
items.why: Powerplant is his stated focus and detonation is the first question most systems-focused examiners ask.

items.x: Not an acronym. The term is preignition.
items.d: Preignition occurs when the fuel-air mixture ignites before the normal ignition event, usually from a residual hot spot such as a glowing carbon deposit or a cracked spark plug insulator. It causes a loss of power and very high operating temperatures. Expect to be asked to distinguish it from detonation, since detonation is a timing-correct burn that goes explosive while preignition is an early light-off.
items.reg: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, FAA-H-8083-25, Chapter 7, Aircraft Systems
items.why: Always paired with detonation on a powerplant-focused oral.

items.x: Not an acronym. The term is spark plug fouling.
items.d: Fouling occurs when low engine operating temperatures are combined with an over-rich mixture, so lead and carbon deposits bridge the spark plug electrodes and the plug stops firing. You prevent it by leaning aggressively for taxi and ground operations in the carbureted Lycoming O-320. It is the most common cause of a rough magneto drop at run-up, and the fix in flight is to lean the mixture and run at higher power briefly.
items.reg: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, FAA-H-8083-25, Chapter 7, Aircraft Systems
items.why: Directly in his ignition and powerplant focus, and it is the likely cause of a run-up discrepancy he will pose as a scenario.

items.x: Not an acronym. The term is magneto, from magneto-electric generator.
items.d: A magneto is an engine-driven electrical generator that uses permanent magnets to produce periodic pulses of alternating current for the spark plugs. It generates current completely independently of the aircraft electrical system and it operates whenever the crankshaft is rotating, which is why a broken or disconnected P-lead can let the engine fire even with the ignition switch OFF. The Warrior has two magnetos feeding two plugs per cylinder, which gives redundancy, a more complete burn, and more power.
items.reg: 14 CFR Part 91, Subpart E, Section 91.409, Inspections; Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, FAA-H-8083-25, Chapter 7, Aircraft Systems
items.why: The classic electrical-versus-ignition trap question and squarely in his focus areas.

items.x: P stands for primary. The P-lead is the primary lead, the ground wire between the magneto and the ignition switch.
items.d: The P-lead grounds out the magneto's primary circuit so that the magneto stops producing spark when the ignition switch is in OFF or when the opposite magneto is selected. If the P-lead is broken or disconnected the magneto is hot at all times, and the Gold Seal guide warns that the engine could start if the propeller is moved with residual fuel in the lines. You check this with the magneto grounding check at idle before shutdown.
items.reg: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, FAA-H-8083-25, Chapter 7, Aircraft Systems
items.why: The standard follow-up to the magneto question and a hands-on safety item in his focus area.

items.x: Not an acronym. The term is fuel-air mixture ratio.
items.d: The fuel-air mixture is the ratio of the weight of fuel to the weight of air in the charge to be burned. Leaning at cruise altitude restores the correct ratio as air density falls and gives optimal engine performance and fuel economy, and leaning before taxi keeps the spark plugs from fouling. The Warrior's carburetor meters by volume, not by mass, so the pilot must lean manually as density altitude increases.
items.reg: Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, FAA-H-8083-25, Chapter 7, Aircraft Systems
items.why: Fuel system management is one of his four named focus areas.

items.x: Not an acronym. The term is carburetor icing, countered by carburetor heat.
items.d: Fuel vaporization and the pressure drop through the venturi of a float-type carburetor can cool the induction air by many degrees and freeze moisture into ice in the throat, which restricts airflow. In a fixed-pitch airplane such as the Warrior the first symptom is a gradual, unexplained drop in RPM with rough running. Carburetor heat routes unfiltered air warmed by an exhaust shroud into the induction system, and applying it causes an immediate further RPM drop followed by a rise and smoothing as the ice melts.
items.reg: 14 CFR Part 91, Subpart A, Section 91.9, Civil aircraft flight manual, marking, and placard requirements; Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, FAA-H-8083-25, Chapter 7, Aircraft Systems
items.why: The Warrior's Lycoming O-320 is carbureted, so an induction-system examiner will go here immediately.

items.x: Not an acronym. The Warrior uses a wet-sump, pressure lubrication system.
items.d: Engine oil lubricates, cools, cleans, seals and cushions, and it carries contaminants to the full-flow filter. The Warrior II POH, Piper Report VB-1180, gives an engine oil capacity of 8 quarts with a minimum safe quantity of 2 quarts, oil and filter change every 50 hours not to exceed 4 months, maximum oil temperature 245 degrees Fahrenheit, oil pressure red lines at 25 PSI minimum and 100 PSI maximum, and a green arc of 60 to 90 PSI. Confirm these in this airplane's POH, because serial 28-8116257 is covered by the earlier Piper Report VB-880 rather than VB-1180.
items.reg: 14 CFR Part 91, Subpart A, Section 91.9, Civil aircraft flight manual, marking, and placard requirements; 14 CFR Part 43, Appendix A, Preventive maintenance
items.why: Oil is the first of his four named focus areas and he will ask for capacities and red lines.

items.x: Not an acronym. The Warrior uses a gravity-assisted, two-tank, selector-fed system with an engine-driven pump and an electric boost pump.
items.d: The Warrior II POH, Piper Report VB-1180, gives a total fuel capacity of 50 US gallons, 2 gallons unusable, 48 gallons usable at 24 gallons per wing, minimum grade 100 or 100LL aviation gasoline, and fuel pressure red lines of 0.5 PSI minimum and 8 PSI maximum with a green arc of 0.5 to 8 PSI. The electric fuel pump is turned on for takeoff, landing and tank switching so that an engine-driven pump failure does not stop fuel flow. Confirm the figures in this airplane's POH, since serial 28-8116257 falls under the earlier Piper Report VB-880.
items.reg: 14 CFR Part 91, Subpart A, Section 91.9, Civil aircraft flight manual, marking, and placard requirements; 14 CFR Part 91, Subpart B, Section 91.151, Fuel requirements for flight in VFR conditions
items.why: Fuel is a named focus area and quantities and grades are checkable facts.

items.x: Not an acronym. The Warrior uses a 14-volt direct current, alternator-driven, single-bus system.
items.d: The Warrior II POH, Piper Report VB-1180, describes a 14-volt, 60-amp alternator, a 12-volt battery mounted in a box on the forward right face of the firewall, a voltage regulator, an overvoltage relay and a master switch relay, with circuit breakers on the lower right instrument panel and an annunciator panel carrying alternator and low oil pressure lights. The alternator supplies all electrical load in flight and charges the battery, the regulator holds bus voltage steady, and the overvoltage relay trips the alternator offline if output runs away. Confirm the ratings in this airplane's POH, since serial 28-8116257 falls under the earlier Piper Report VB-880.
items.reg: 14 CFR Part 91, Subpart A, Section 91.9, Civil aircraft flight manual, marking, and placard requirements
items.why: Electrical is a named focus area and he will want the alternator rating, the bus voltage and the failure indications.

items.x: G - Gas. U - Undercarriage. M - Mixture. P - Propeller. S - Switches, seat belts and safety.
items.d: GUMPS is the standard pre-landing flow, run on downwind and again on final, to make sure the airplane is configured to land. In the Warrior the gear is fixed and the propeller is fixed-pitch, so U becomes a confirmation that the gear is welded down and P is not applicable, but you still say the whole flow out loud because an examiner wants the habit pattern that transfers to a retractable. This mnemonic does not appear in the Gold Seal guide; it is a widely taught industry flow rather than a regulation.
items.why: He will fly the power-off 180 and he will want a verbalized pre-landing flow that covers fuel selector and mixture.

items.x: Not an acronym. The term is fixed-pitch propeller.
items.d: On a fixed-pitch propeller the blade angle is built into the blade itself and cannot be changed once the propeller is manufactured, so the pilot has one power control, the throttle, and engine RPM varies with airspeed and power. The Warrior II uses a Sensenich fixed-pitch propeller per Piper Report VB-1180. A fixed-pitch propeller is efficient only at one combination of airspeed and RPM, which is why it is specified as either a climb or a cruise propeller.
items.reg: 14 CFR Part 91, Subpart A, Section 91.9, Civil aircraft flight manual, marking, and placard requirements
items.why: It is what he is flying and it sets up the contrast with the constant-speed propeller required for the complex training.

items.x: Not an acronym. The term is constant-speed, or controllable-pitch, propeller.
items.d: A constant-speed propeller is a controllable-pitch propeller whose blade angle is varied automatically in flight by a governor, so the pilot has two controls, the throttle for manifold pressure and the propeller control for RPM. Once an RPM is selected the governor adjusts blade angle to hold it as airspeed and power change. The commercial applicant must have at least 10 hours of complex or technically advanced airplane training, so expect the oval of manifold-pressure-and-RPM sequencing questions even in a fixed-pitch airplane.
items.reg: 14 CFR Part 61, Subpart F, Section 61.129, Aeronautical experience; 14 CFR Part 61, Subpart A, Section 61.31, Type rating requirements, additional training, and authorization requirements
items.why: Commercial training requires complex or TAA time, and it is the natural powerplant follow-up to the fixed-pitch answer.

items.x: R - Revolutions. P - Per. M - Minute.
items.d: RPM is the rotational speed of the crankshaft and, on a fixed-pitch airplane, of the propeller. It is the Warrior pilot's only direct power indication, with a tachometer green arc of 500 to 2700 RPM and a red line of 2700 RPM at maximum continuous power per the POH. A magneto check on run-up is judged by the RPM drop on each magneto and the difference between them, and an unexplained RPM loss in cruise points toward carburetor ice.
items.reg: 14 CFR Part 91, Subpart C, Section 91.205, Powered civil aircraft with standard category U.S. airworthiness certificates: Instrument and equipment requirements
items.why: It is the single power indication in his airplane and the measurement behind every run-up discrepancy question.

items.x: M - Manifold. P - Pressure.
items.d: Manifold pressure is the absolute pressure of the air in the intake manifold downstream of the throttle, read in inches of mercury, and it is the power indication on a constant-speed installation. It is the M in A TOMATO FLAMES, but Section 91.205 requires a manifold pressure gauge only for each altitude engine, so a normally aspirated fixed-pitch Warrior does not carry one and is not required to. Knowing why your airplane lacks an item on the required list is a standard examiner probe.
items.reg: 14 CFR Part 91, Subpart C, Section 91.205, Powered civil aircraft with standard category U.S. airworthiness certificates: Instrument and equipment requirements
items.why: The required-equipment list and his powerplant focus intersect exactly here.

items.x: AV - Aviation. GAS - Gasoline.
items.d: Aviation gasoline is the spark-ignition piston fuel, graded by octane and dyed by grade, with 100LL dyed blue and 100 dyed green. The Warrior II POH specifies AVGAS only, minimum grade 100 or 100LL, and warns that lower grades can cause serious engine damage. During preflight you sump each tank and the strainer to check for the right color, water and sediment.
items.reg: 14 CFR Part 91, Subpart A, Section 91.9, Civil aircraft flight manual, marking, and placard requirements
items.why: Fuel grade and color is a near-certain question on a fuel-focused oral.

items.x: C - Controls free and correct. I - Instruments set and checked. G - Gas, correct tank, quantity and fuel pump. A - Attitude, meaning trim and flaps set for takeoff. R - Run-up and radios complete.
items.d: CIGAR is the traditional pre-takeoff check flow used to confirm the airplane is ready for departure. The common variant CIGARS or CIGARTIP adds S for seat belts and switches and TIP for transponder, interior and pitot heat. This mnemonic does not appear in the Gold Seal guide and it is not regulatory; it is a memory aid that backs up the POH checklist, which is the controlling document.
items.reg: 14 CFR Part 91, Subpart A, Section 91.9, Civil aircraft flight manual, marking, and placard requirements
items.why: Likely as a flow question, but the POH checklist is what an examiner holds you to.

items.x: Not an acronym. The term is engine-driven vacuum, or suction, system.
items.d: An engine-driven vacuum pump draws filtered cabin air across the rotors of the attitude indicator and heading indicator to spin them, and the gauge shows suction in inches of mercury. A vacuum failure takes those two gyroscopic instruments with it while the electrically driven turn coordinator and the pitot-static instruments keep working. The Warrior II POH lists a low vacuum annunciator light when the optional gyro system is installed.
items.reg: 14 CFR Part 91, Subpart C, Section 91.205, Powered civil aircraft with standard category U.S. airworthiness certificates: Instrument and equipment requirements
items.why: A systems examiner uses it to test partial-panel reasoning, but it sits just outside his four named areas.

items.x: B - Brake. H - Horse. P - Power.
items.d: Brake horsepower is the actual power delivered at the propeller shaft, measured as the power the engine can deliver against a brake, as distinct from indicated or friction horsepower. The Warrior II POH lists a maximum of 160 horsepower at 2700 RPM for the Lycoming O-320-D2A or O-320-D3G. It matters because the high-performance endorsement threshold under Section 61.31 is an engine of more than 200 horsepower, which the Warrior is well under.
items.reg: 14 CFR Part 61, Subpart A, Section 61.31, Type rating requirements, additional training, and authorization requirements
items.why: Listed on page 31 and it links his powerplant focus to the endorsement question.

items.x: G - Gallons. P - Per. H - Hour.
items.d: Gallons per hour is the volumetric fuel consumption rate used for endurance and range planning in a piston airplane. You use it with usable fuel to compute endurance, and with groundspeed to compute range, including the Section 91.151 VFR reserve of 30 minutes by day and 45 minutes at night at normal cruising speed. Read the figure from the POH cruise performance charts for the power setting and altitude you are actually flying.
items.reg: 14 CFR Part 91, Subpart B, Section 91.151, Fuel requirements for flight in VFR conditions
items.why: Listed on page 31 and it is how a fuel-focused examiner moves from systems into planning.

items.x: T - Time. B - Between. O - Overhaul.
items.d: Time between overhaul is the manufacturer's recommended operating hours or calendar time before the engine is overhauled. Under Part 91 the TBO is a recommendation, not a limitation, so an engine past TBO can still be airworthy provided it meets its inspection requirements and remains in a condition for safe operation. This term is not in the Gold Seal guide, but a systems-focused examiner often uses it to test whether you know the difference between a manufacturer recommendation and a regulatory requirement.
items.reg: 14 CFR Part 91, Subpart E, Section 91.409, Inspections; 14 CFR Part 91, Subpart A, Section 91.7, Civil aircraft airworthiness
items.why: A favorite trap for systems examiners because it separates recommendation from regulation.

items.x: EGT: E - Exhaust. G - Gas. T - Temperature. CHT: C - Cylinder. H - Head. T - Temperature.
items.d: Exhaust gas temperature measures the temperature of the exhaust stream and is used as the reference for leaning, since peak EGT marks the chemically correct mixture and you then set a specific number of degrees rich of peak or lean of peak. Cylinder head temperature measures the metal temperature of the cylinder head and is the limit that protects the engine from thermal damage. Neither is required equipment under Section 91.205 for this airplane, and the Warrior may or may not have them installed, so check the panel.
items.reg: 14 CFR Part 91, Subpart C, Section 91.205, Powered civil aircraft with standard category U.S. airworthiness certificates: Instrument and equipment requirements
items.why: Leaning technique is a standard powerplant question even when the gauges are optional.

items.x: P - Pounds. P - Per. H - Hour.
items.d: Pounds per hour is the mass fuel consumption rate, used mainly for turbine airplanes and for weight and balance work where fuel burn must be converted to a weight change. For a piston airplane you convert from gallons per hour using 6 pounds per gallon for aviation gasoline. It appears on page 31 of the guide as a general abbreviation.
items.why: On the page 31 list but rarely asked on a piston single ride.

groups.g: Required Documents, Equipment and Preflight Action

items.x: A - Altimeter. T - Tachometer for each engine. O - Oil temperature gauge for each engine. M - Manifold pressure gauge for each engine. A - Airspeed indicator. T - Temperature gauge for each liquid-cooled engine. O - Oil pressure gauge for each engine. F - Fuel quantity gauge for each fuel tank. L - Landing gear position lights. A - Anticollision lights. M - Magnetic compass. E - Emergency locator transmitter. S - Safety belts and shoulder harnesses.
items.d: This is the minimum instrument and equipment list for day VFR flight in a standard category airplane. Several items are conditional: the manifold pressure gauge applies to each altitude engine, the liquid-cooled temperature gauge applies only to liquid-cooled engines, landing gear position lights apply only to retractable gear, and anticollision lights are required on aircraft certificated after 11 March 1996. The common variant is ATOMATOFLAMES run together, and some instructors use the longer TOMATO FLAMES A FLAPS; the Gold Seal guide prints A TOMATO FLAMES.
items.reg: 14 CFR Part 91, Subpart C, Section 91.205, Powered civil aircraft with standard category U.S. airworthiness certificates: Instrument and equipment requirements, paragraph (b)
items.why: A checkoff item on every ride, and half its letters are oil, fuel and powerplant instruments he already wants to talk about.

items.x: F - Fuses, a spare set, or circuit breakers. L - Landing light, required only if the aircraft is operated for hire. A - Anticollision lights. P - Position lights, also called navigation lights. S - Source of electrical power, such as a battery or alternator.
items.d: FLAPS is what you add to the day VFR list for night VFR flight. The landing light requirement is conditional on operating for hire, which is precisely the commercial pilot's situation, so expect the follow-up about carrying passengers for compensation at night. The S for source of power ties straight into the Warrior's alternator and battery.
items.reg: 14 CFR Part 91, Subpart C, Section 91.205, Powered civil aircraft with standard category U.S. airworthiness certificates: Instrument and equipment requirements, paragraph (c)
items.why: Required-item mnemonic, and the for-hire landing light clause plus the S for electrical source land in two of his focus areas.

items.x: G - Generator or alternator of adequate capacity. R - Radios, two-way communication and navigation equipment appropriate to the ground facilities to be used. A - Altimeter, pressure sensitive and adjustable. B - Ball, the slip-skid indicator. C - Clock, installed, showing hours, minutes and seconds with a sweep-second pointer or digital presentation. A - Attitude indicator. R - Rate of turn indicator. D - Directional gyro, the heading indicator.
items.d: GRABCARD is what you add to the day VFR list, plus FLAPS if at night, for instrument flight. The G is an alternator or generator of adequate capacity for the installed equipment, which is why the Warrior's 60-amp alternator rating matters. Note that the regulation uses the phrase gyroscopic rate-of-turn indicator and a slip-skid indicator rather than the plain words ball and rate of turn.
items.reg: 14 CFR Part 91, Subpart C, Section 91.205, Powered civil aircraft with standard category U.S. airworthiness certificates: Instrument and equipment requirements, paragraph (d)
items.why: Required-item mnemonic and the G is an electrical question in disguise.

items.x: A - Airworthiness certificate. R - Registration certificate. R - Radio station license, required only for international flights. O - Operating limitations and information, which is the approved flight manual, placards, markings and any required supplements. W - Weight and balance data specific to that aircraft.
items.d: ARROW is the set of documents that must be aboard the aircraft. The Gold Seal guide heads this box with Sections 21.5, 91.103, 91.1 and 91.203, and that citation is partly wrong: the documents requirement is Section 91.203 for the airworthiness and registration certificates and Section 91.9 for the operating limitations, while Section 91.103 is preflight action and has nothing to do with onboard paperwork. Cite Sections 91.203 and 91.9, and Section 21.5 for the flight manual delivery requirement.
items.reg: 14 CFR Part 91, Subpart C, Section 91.203, Civil aircraft: Certifications required; 14 CFR Part 91, Subpart A, Section 91.9, Civil aircraft flight manual, marking, and placard requirements; 14 CFR Part 21, Subpart A, Section 21.5, Airplane or Rotorcraft Flight Manual
items.why: Pure checkoff item, asked on essentially every practical test before the airplane is even looked at.

items.x: N - NOTAMs. W - Weather reports and forecasts. K - Known air traffic delays advised by ATC. R - Runway lengths at the airports of intended use. A - Alternates available if the flight cannot be completed as planned. F - Fuel requirements. T - Takeoff and landing distance data.
items.d: This is the preflight action required before beginning any flight, and for a flight not in the vicinity of an airport it adds the runway, alternate, fuel and performance items. The Gold Seal guide labels this box Preflight Info Required for IFR, which is too narrow; Section 91.103 applies to every flight, and the extended list applies to any IFR flight or any flight not in the vicinity of an airport. Common variants are NWKRAFT and WKRAFT run together; the guide prints NW KRAFT.
items.reg: 14 CFR Part 91, Subpart B, Section 91.103, Preflight action
items.why: Required-item mnemonic with a regulation an examiner can read aloud, and its F and T feed fuel and performance questions.

items.x: E - Emergency. L - Locator. T - Transmitter.
items.d: The emergency locator transmitter is a crash-activated beacon required for most Part 91 airplanes, inspected every 12 calendar months. The battery must be replaced or recharged after more than 1 cumulative hour of use, or when 50 percent of its useful life has expired. It is the E in A TOMATO FLAMES and the E in AV1ATES.
items.reg: 14 CFR Part 91, Subpart C, Section 91.207, Emergency locator transmitters
items.why: It appears in two required-item mnemonics and carries its own battery rule that examiners love to check.

items.x: M - Minimum. E - Equipment. L - List.
items.d: A minimum equipment list is an FAA-approved document, specific to the operator and aircraft, that permits flight with specified equipment inoperative under stated conditions and procedures. If the aircraft has an approved MEL you follow the MEL and the Section 91.213 paragraph (d) placard-or-remove path does not apply. Most Part 91 training airplanes, including a typical Warrior, have no MEL and operate under Section 91.213 paragraph (d) instead.
items.reg: 14 CFR Part 91, Subpart C, Section 91.213, Inoperative instruments and equipment
items.why: Inoperative equipment is standard airworthiness territory and he will push on which path applies to this airplane.

items.x: K - Kinds. O - of. E - Equipment. L - List. The full title is Kinds of Operation Equipment List.
items.d: The kinds of operation equipment list is the POH table, in Section 2 Limitations, that names the systems and equipment on which type certification for day VFR, night VFR, day IFR and night IFR was predicated and which must be installed and operable for each kind of operation. The Warrior II list for day VFR includes the airspeed indicator, altimeter, magnetic compass, tachometer, oil pressure and oil temperature indicators, fuel pressure and fuel quantity indicators, volt-ammeter, trim indicator, alternator and restraints. It is the fourth branch of the Section 91.213 inoperative equipment decision tree.
items.reg: 14 CFR Part 91, Subpart C, Section 91.213, Inoperative instruments and equipment; 14 CFR Part 91, Subpart A, Section 91.9, Civil aircraft flight manual, marking, and placard requirements
items.why: It lives in his airplane's POH and it lists oil, fuel and electrical instruments by name.

items.x: Not an acronym.
items.d: With an item inoperative and no MEL, you ask in turn whether the equipment is required by an airworthiness directive, by the regulations for the kind of operation being conducted, by the VFR-day type certification requirements in the KOEL, or by an operational equipment list. If the answer to any of those is yes, the airplane may not fly without a special flight permit. If all are no, the item must be removed or deactivated and placarded inoperative, and a pilot or mechanic must determine the aircraft is safe to fly.
items.reg: 14 CFR Part 91, Subpart C, Section 91.213, Inoperative instruments and equipment
items.why: He will hand you a broken oil pressure gauge or a dead ammeter and ask whether you can go.

items.x: A - Automatic. D - Dependent. S - Surveillance. B - Broadcast. Out means the aircraft transmits.
items.d: ADS-B Out equipment automatically broadcasts the aircraft's GPS position, altitude, velocity and identity without pilot action or interrogation. It is required in Class A, B and C airspace, within the Mode C veil, in Class E at or above 10,000 feet MSL excluding airspace at and below 2,500 feet AGL, above the ceiling and within the lateral limits of Class B or Class C up to 10,000 feet MSL, and in Class E over the Gulf of Mexico at and above 3,000 feet MSL within 12 nautical miles of the coast.
items.reg: 14 CFR Part 91, Subpart C, Section 91.225, Automatic Dependent Surveillance-Broadcast (ADS-B) Out equipment and use
items.why: An equipment rule he can check, though it is airspace rather than systems.

items.x: Not an acronym. Mode C refers to the altitude-reporting transponder mode.
items.d: The Mode C veil is the airspace within 30 nautical miles of a Class B primary airport, from the surface to 10,000 feet MSL, in which an altitude-reporting transponder and ADS-B Out are required. You need to know whether your home field sits inside one and what to do if the transponder fails en route.
items.reg: 14 CFR Part 91, Subpart C, Section 91.215, ATC transponder and altitude reporting equipment and use; 14 CFR Part 91, Subpart C, Section 91.225, Automatic Dependent Surveillance-Broadcast (ADS-B) Out equipment and use
items.why: Standard airspace equipment follow-up, one step away from his focus.

items.x: Not an acronym. Also called a ferry permit.
items.d: A special flight permit is issued by the FAA under Part 21 for an aircraft that does not currently meet applicable airworthiness requirements but is capable of safe flight, typically to fly the airplane to a base where repairs will be made. It is the exit the Section 91.213 flowchart points to when required equipment is inoperative. You apply through your Flight Standards District Office or a designated airworthiness representative.
items.reg: 14 CFR Part 21, Subpart H, Section 21.197, Special flight permits; 14 CFR Part 91, Subpart C, Section 91.213, Inoperative instruments and equipment
items.why: The natural second half of the inoperative equipment answer.

items.x: A - Annual inspection, every 12 calendar months. V - VOR equipment check, every 30 days, for IFR operations. 1 - 100-hour inspection, required when carrying persons for hire or giving flight instruction for hire in a provided aircraft. A - Altimeter and static pressure system, every 24 calendar months. T - Transponder, every 24 calendar months. E - Emergency locator transmitter, every 12 calendar months. S - Static system, every 24 calendar months.
items.d: AV1ATES is the list of recurring inspections and checks that keep an aircraft legal. Two cautions the Gold Seal guide glosses over: the VOR check is only a requirement for IFR operations under Section 91.171 and is not an airworthiness inspection at all, and the altimeter and static system checks are the same Section 91.411 inspection, so the A and the S are not two independent items. Common variants are AVIATES and AV1ATE; the guide prints AV1ATES with the numeral one.
items.reg: 14 CFR Part 91, Subpart E, Section 91.409, Inspections; 14 CFR Part 91, Subpart E, Section 91.411, Altimeter system and altitude reporting equipment tests and inspections; 14 CFR Part 91, Subpart E, Section 91.413, ATC transponder tests and inspections; 14 CFR Part 91, Subpart C, Section 91.207, Emergency locator transmitters; 14 CFR Part 91, Subpart B, Section 91.171, VOR equipment check for IFR operations
items.why: The single most reliable checkoff mnemonic on any practical test, and the 100-hour clause goes straight to commercial for-hire operations.

items.x: Not an acronym.
items.d: A 100-hour inspection is required when an aircraft is carrying any person other than a crewmember for hire, or when it is giving flight instruction for hire and the operator provides the aircraft. It may be exceeded by not more than 10 hours only to reach a place where the inspection can be done, and the excess is then subtracted from the next 100-hour interval. The 100-hour is the item that turns a private airplane into a commercial one, so it is the commercial applicant's inspection.
items.reg: 14 CFR Part 91, Subpart E, Section 91.409, Inspections, paragraph (b)
items.why: It is the inspection that exists because of commercial privileges, and it has a 10-hour exception he can test.

items.x: Not an acronym.
items.d: No person may operate an aircraft unless, within the preceding 12 calendar months, it has had an annual inspection and been approved for return to service by a person authorized under Part 43. An annual satisfies the 100-hour requirement, but a 100-hour does not satisfy an annual, because only an inspection authorization holder may sign an annual. Twelve calendar months means through the last day of the twelfth month.
items.reg: 14 CFR Part 91, Subpart E, Section 91.409, Inspections, paragraph (a); 14 CFR Part 43, Section 43.7, Persons authorized to approve aircraft, airframes, aircraft engines, propellers, appliances, or component parts for return to service
items.why: Checkoff item on every ride and the setup for the annual-versus-100-hour distinction.

items.x: A - Airworthiness. D - Directive.
items.d: An airworthiness directive is a legally enforceable rule issued by the FAA under Part 39 to correct an unsafe condition in a product. Compliance is mandatory, ADs may be one-time or recurring, and an aircraft with an overdue AD is unairworthy. The pilot in command is responsible for determining the aircraft is airworthy, which means knowing that the AD status has been checked, though the records themselves are normally the owner's responsibility.
items.reg: 14 CFR Part 39, Section 39.3, Definition of airworthiness directives; 14 CFR Part 91, Subpart A, Section 91.403, General; 14 CFR Part 91, Subpart A, Section 91.7, Civil aircraft airworthiness
items.why: It is the first branch of the Section 91.213 flowchart and a standard airworthiness certainty.

items.x: Not an acronym. The two-part definition is conformity plus safe condition.
items.d: An aircraft is airworthy when it conforms to its type certificate, including any supplemental type certificates and complied-with airworthiness directives, and when it is in a condition for safe operation. The pilot in command is responsible for determining whether the aircraft is in condition for safe flight and must discontinue the flight when unairworthy conditions occur. The Gold Seal guide states correctly that confirmation of airworthiness is the responsibility of the pilot in command.
items.reg: 14 CFR Part 91, Subpart A, Section 91.7, Civil aircraft airworthiness; 14 CFR Part 3, Section 3.5, Statements about products, parts, appliances and materials
items.why: The umbrella question that every inspection and equipment answer hangs from.

items.x: S - Supplemental. T - Type. C - Certificate.
items.d: A supplemental type certificate approves a major change to a type-certificated product, such as an avionics installation, an auto-gas approval or a gross weight increase, and it becomes part of the aircraft's approved configuration. An STC brings its own flight manual supplement, which then belongs with the O in ARROW. This term is not on pages 31 and 32 of the Gold Seal guide.
items.reg: 14 CFR Part 21, Subpart E, Section 21.113, Requirement for supplemental type certificate
items.why: Likely when he asks what makes the airplane conform to its type design.

items.x: Not an acronym.
items.d: Preventive maintenance is the list of simple or minor preservation operations and small standard part replacements in Part 43 Appendix A paragraph (c), which a certificated pilot holding at least a private pilot certificate may perform on an aircraft they own or operate, provided the aircraft is not operated under Parts 121, 129 or 135. Servicing the battery, changing the oil and filter, replacing safety belts and replacing landing light bulbs are on the list, and the work must be recorded in the maintenance records. This term is not on pages 31 and 32 of the Gold Seal guide.
items.reg: 14 CFR Part 43, Appendix A, paragraph (c), Preventive maintenance; 14 CFR Part 43, Section 43.3, Persons authorized to perform maintenance, preventive maintenance, rebuilding, and alterations; 14 CFR Part 43, Section 43.9, Content, form, and disposition of maintenance, preventive maintenance, rebuilding, and alteration records
items.why: Oil changes and battery servicing are preventive maintenance, which puts this directly in his oil and electrical focus.

items.x: T - Type. C - Certificate. D - Data. S - Sheet.
items.d: The type certificate data sheet is the FAA document that defines the approved configuration and limitations of the type, including approved engines and propellers, fuel grades, placards and control surface travels. You use it to decide whether a given part or modification is approved for the airframe. This term is not on pages 31 and 32 of the Gold Seal guide.
items.reg: 14 CFR Part 21, Subpart B, Section 21.41, Type certificate
items.why: Possible on a thorough airworthiness line of questioning, but usually left to maintenance.

items.x: Not an acronym.
items.d: When an aircraft has undergone maintenance, preventive maintenance, rebuilding or alteration that may have appreciably changed its flight characteristics or substantially affected its operation in flight, no person may carry any person other than a crewmember until an appropriately rated pilot holding at least a private pilot certificate has flown the aircraft, made an operational check and logged the flight in the maintenance records. The Gold Seal guide states this correctly on page 5.
items.reg: 14 CFR Part 91, Subpart E, Section 91.407, Operation after maintenance, preventive maintenance, rebuilding, or alteration, paragraph (b)
items.why: A niche but checkable rule that a maintenance-minded examiner sometimes reaches for.

items.x: V - Velocity. A - Design maneuvering.
items.d: Design maneuvering speed is the maximum speed at which full or abrupt movement of a single flight control will cause the airplane to stall before the structure is overstressed. It is airframe-dependent and also weight-dependent, decreasing as weight decreases. The Warrior II POH, Piper Report VB-1180, gives 111 KIAS at 2440 pounds and 88 KIAS at 1531 pounds with linear interpolation between, but serial 28-8116257 is covered by the earlier Piper Report VB-880, so confirm in this airplane's POH.
items.reg: 14 CFR Part 23, Section 23.2005, Certification of normal category airplanes; 14 CFR Part 91, Subpart A, Section 91.9, Civil aircraft flight manual, marking, and placard requirements
items.why: The one V-speed that is weight-dependent and not marked on the airspeed indicator, so it is asked on nearly every ride.

items.x: V - Velocity. N - Never. E - Exceed.
items.d: Never exceed speed is the speed that may not be exceeded in any operation, marked by the red radial line at the top of the airspeed indicator. Above it structural failure or flutter is possible. It is airframe-dependent; the Warrior II POH, Piper Report VB-1180, gives 160 KIAS, which is 153 KCAS, but confirm in this airplane's POH because serial 28-8116257 falls under Piper Report VB-880.
items.reg: 14 CFR Part 91, Subpart A, Section 91.9, Civil aircraft flight manual, marking, and placard requirements
items.why: Part of the airspeed indicator markings walk that opens most orals.

items.x: V - Velocity. N - Normal. O - Operating. Also called maximum structural cruising speed.
items.d: Maximum structural cruising speed is the top of the green arc and the bottom of the yellow caution arc, and it may be exceeded only in smooth air and then only with caution. It is airframe-dependent; the Warrior II POH, Piper Report VB-1180, gives 126 KIAS, which is 122 KCAS. Confirm in this airplane's POH, since serial 28-8116257 is covered by Piper Report VB-880.
items.reg: 14 CFR Part 91, Subpart A, Section 91.9, Civil aircraft flight manual, marking, and placard requirements
items.why: Half of the arc explanation and a standard turbulence-penetration question.

items.x: V - Velocity. F - Flap. E - Extended.
items.d: Maximum flap extended speed is the highest speed at which the flaps may be flown in an extended position, marked by the top of the white arc. Exceeding it risks structural damage to the flaps and their attachments. It is airframe-dependent; the Warrior II POH, Piper Report VB-1180, gives 103 KIAS, which is 100 KCAS, and marks the white arc from 44 to 103 KIAS. Confirm in this airplane's POH.
items.reg: 14 CFR Part 91, Subpart A, Section 91.9, Civil aircraft flight manual, marking, and placard requirements
items.why: Part of the arcs walk and directly relevant to the power-off 180 and short-field landings.

items.x: V - Velocity. S - Stall. O - Zero, meaning flaps and gear in the landing configuration.
items.d: Stall speed or minimum steady flight speed in the landing configuration, at maximum gross weight, is the bottom of the white arc. It is airframe-dependent and varies with weight, bank angle and load factor. The Warrior II POH, Piper Report VB-1180, marks the white arc beginning at 44 KIAS; confirm the published stall speeds in this airplane's POH, since serial 28-8116257 falls under Piper Report VB-880.
items.reg: 14 CFR Part 91, Subpart A, Section 91.9, Civil aircraft flight manual, marking, and placard requirements
items.why: Bottom of the white arc, asked in the same breath as VFE.

items.x: V - Velocity. S - Stall. 1 - A specified configuration, normally clean, with flaps and gear retracted.
items.d: Stall speed in a specified configuration, normally the clean configuration at maximum gross weight, is the bottom of the green arc. The Warrior II POH, Piper Report VB-1180, marks the green arc beginning at 50 KIAS. It is airframe-dependent and rises with weight, bank and load factor, which is the point an examiner is driving at when he asks what happens to stall speed in a steep turn. Confirm in this airplane's POH.
items.reg: 14 CFR Part 91, Subpart A, Section 91.9, Civil aircraft flight manual, marking, and placard requirements
items.why: Bottom of the green arc and the lead-in to accelerated stall questions on chandelles and lazy eights.

items.x: V - Velocity. X - Best angle of climb.
items.d: Best angle of climb speed gives the greatest altitude gain per unit of horizontal distance, so it is the obstacle-clearance speed used on a short-field takeoff. It is airframe-dependent and increases slightly with altitude. The Warrior II POH, Piper Report VB-1180, Section 4, gives 63 KIAS; confirm in this airplane's POH, since serial 28-8116257 falls under Piper Report VB-880.
items.reg: 14 CFR Part 91, Subpart A, Section 91.9, Civil aircraft flight manual, marking, and placard requirements; FAA-S-ACS-7, Commercial Pilot for Airplane Category Airman Certification Standards
items.why: Required for the short-field takeoff task and he will ask how VX and VY converge with altitude.

items.x: V - Velocity. Y - Best rate of climb.
items.d: Best rate of climb speed gives the greatest altitude gain per unit of time, so it is the normal climb speed once obstacles are cleared. It is airframe-dependent and decreases slightly with altitude, converging with VX at the absolute ceiling. The Warrior II POH, Piper Report VB-1180, Section 4, gives 79 KIAS at gross weight; confirm in this airplane's POH.
items.reg: 14 CFR Part 91, Subpart A, Section 91.9, Civil aircraft flight manual, marking, and placard requirements; FAA-S-ACS-7, Commercial Pilot for Airplane Category Airman Certification Standards
items.why: Flown on every takeoff and paired with VX in the convergence question.

items.x: V - Velocity. G - Glide. Commonly written as best glide speed rather than as a certification symbol.
items.d: Best glide speed is the airspeed that produces the maximum lift-to-drag ratio and therefore the greatest glide distance per foot of altitude lost. It is airframe-dependent and varies with weight, decreasing as weight decreases. The Warrior II POH, Piper Report VB-1180, uses 73 KIAS for glide performance at 2440 pounds with the propeller windmilling and flaps up, and the engine power loss in flight procedure says to trim for 73 KIAS; confirm in this airplane's POH.
items.reg: 14 CFR Part 91, Subpart A, Section 91.9, Civil aircraft flight manual, marking, and placard requirements; FAA-S-ACS-7, Commercial Pilot for Airplane Category Airman Certification Standards
items.why: The engine failure and steep spiral speed, and a powerplant-focused examiner reaches engine failure quickly.

items.t: VFE and the Airspeed Indicator Arcs
items.x: Not an acronym. White arc, green arc, yellow arc, red radial line.
items.d: The white arc is the flap operating range, from VSO at the bottom to VFE at the top. The green arc is the normal operating range, from VS1 at the bottom to VNO at the top. The yellow arc is the caution range, from VNO to VNE, to be flown only in smooth air and with caution. The red radial line is VNE. The Warrior II POH, Piper Report VB-1180, marks white 44 to 103, green 50 to 126, yellow 126 to 160 and red line 160 KIAS; confirm in this airplane's POH.
items.reg: 14 CFR Part 91, Subpart A, Section 91.9, Civil aircraft flight manual, marking, and placard requirements
items.why: Nearly every oral begins by pointing at the airspeed indicator and asking what each color means.

items.x: V - Velocity. S - Stall.
items.d: Stall speed, used generically for the stalling speed or minimum steady flight speed at which the airplane is controllable. The Gold Seal guide lists it as stall speed, clean configuration. In practice you quote VSO and VS1 because those are the two speeds the airspeed indicator actually marks. Airframe-dependent.
items.reg: 14 CFR Part 91, Subpart A, Section 91.9, Civil aircraft flight manual, marking, and placard requirements
items.why: Usually subsumed by VSO and VS1, but the guide lists it so he may ask you to distinguish them.

items.x: V - Velocity. REF - Reference, meaning the reference landing approach speed.
items.d: VREF is the calculated final approach speed, normally a factor applied to the landing configuration stall speed. The Warrior II POH does not publish a figure labeled VREF; it publishes a landing final approach speed of 63 KIAS with flaps 40 degrees and an initial approach speed of about 70 KIAS, per Piper Report VB-1180, Section 4. Confirm in this airplane's POH, since serial 28-8116257 falls under Piper Report VB-880.
items.reg: 14 CFR Part 91, Subpart A, Section 91.9, Civil aircraft flight manual, marking, and placard requirements
items.why: Likely on the landing tasks, though the Warrior POH does not use the term so the answer is the published approach speed.

items.x: V - Velocity. L - Landing gear. E - Extended.
items.d: Maximum landing gear extended speed is the highest speed at which the airplane may be flown with the landing gear down and locked. It is airframe-dependent and does not apply to the Warrior, which has fixed gear, but you must know it because the commercial certificate contemplates complex airplanes and the examiner may ask about the airplane you did your complex training in.
items.reg: 14 CFR Part 91, Subpart A, Section 91.9, Civil aircraft flight manual, marking, and placard requirements
items.why: Listed in the guide and tied to complex training, but not applicable to the fixed-gear Warrior.

items.x: V - Velocity. L - Landing gear. O - Operating.
items.d: Maximum landing gear operating speed is the highest speed at which the gear may be extended or retracted, and it is often lower than VLE because the gear doors and actuating mechanism see loads during transit. It is airframe-dependent and does not apply to the fixed-gear Warrior. The Gold Seal guide lists VLE but omits VLO; the pair is standard and examiners commonly ask for both.
items.reg: 14 CFR Part 91, Subpart A, Section 91.9, Civil aircraft flight manual, marking, and placard requirements
items.why: The guide omits it, which is exactly why an examiner who notices will ask.

items.x: V - Velocity. F - Flap, meaning design flap speed.
items.d: Design flap speed is the certification speed used in designing the flap structure, as distinct from VFE, which is the operating limit shown to the pilot. You will normally never see VF in a POH; the number you fly to is VFE, the top of the white arc. Airframe-dependent and a certification value rather than an operating limitation.
items.reg: 14 CFR Part 23, Section 23.2005, Certification of normal category airplanes
items.why: On the guide's list but it is a design value, not something he will hold you to.

items.x: Not an acronym.
items.d: Holding out is advertising or otherwise making known to the public a willingness to furnish transportation to anyone who asks. The Gold Seal guide lists agents, word of mouth, advertising and signs, and the internet and social media as ways it can be done. Holding out is the single element that converts carriage for hire into common carriage, which requires an operating certificate.
items.reg: Advisory Circular 120-12A, Private Carriage Versus Common Carriage of Persons or Property; 14 CFR Part 119, Subpart A, Section 119.1, Applicability
items.why: The central concept of the commercial privileges area and he must hear it defined cleanly.

items.x: Not an acronym. The four elements are holding out, transporting persons or property, from place to place, for compensation.
items.d: A carrier becomes a common carrier when it holds itself out to the public as willing to furnish transportation to those who want it. All four elements must be present. Common carriage requires an operating certificate under Part 119 and operation under Part 121 or Part 135, and the IFR takeoff minimums then apply, which they do not under Part 91.
items.reg: Advisory Circular 120-12A, Private Carriage Versus Common Carriage of Persons or Property; 14 CFR Part 119, Subpart A, Section 119.1, Applicability; 14 CFR Part 135, Subpart I, Section 135.225, IFR: Takeoff, approach and landing minimums
items.why: A near-certain commercial oral question and the four elements are a checkable recitation.

items.x: Not an acronym. Also called noncommon carriage.
items.d: Private carriage is carriage for hire that does not involve holding out, typically carriage for one or a small number of contracted customers. The Gold Seal guide describes one aircraft operator working for one or two contracted clients. It can still require a Part 125 or Part 135 certificate depending on the aircraft size and payload, but it is not common carriage.
items.reg: Advisory Circular 120-12A, Private Carriage Versus Common Carriage of Persons or Property; 14 CFR Part 119, Subpart A, Section 119.1, Applicability
items.why: The other half of the carriage question and the one applicants usually fumble.

items.x: Not an acronym.
items.d: Compensation is anything of value, including the sharing of expenses, profit or profit motive, goodwill in the form of expected future economic benefit, the accrual of flight time, and value delivered to a third party recipient. An actual exchange of funds is not required. The practical test the Gold Seal guide offers is that anything that would get you to make the flight when you otherwise would not can be compensation in the eyes of the FAA.
items.reg: Advisory Circular 61-142, Sharing Aircraft Operating Expenses in Accordance with 14 CFR Section 61.113(c); 14 CFR Part 61, Subpart F, Section 61.133, Commercial pilot privileges and limitations
items.why: Every commercial examiner probes whether the applicant understands that logging time can itself be compensation.

items.x: Not an acronym.
items.d: Operational control is the exercise of authority over initiating, conducting or terminating a flight. It is the hinge on which many commercial scenarios turn, because whoever holds operational control is the operator and therefore needs the certificate. A commercial pilot flying an airplane the customer provides, where the customer controls the flight, is in a different position from one who supplies the airplane as well.
items.reg: 14 CFR Part 1, Section 1.1, General definitions; 14 CFR Part 119, Subpart A, Section 119.1, Applicability
items.why: It is how he will test whether you can reason about who needs the certificate.

items.x: Not an acronym.
items.d: Section 119.1 paragraph (e) lists operations that may be conducted for compensation or hire without a Part 119 operating certificate. The Gold Seal guide lists student instruction, nonstop commercial air tours that begin and end at the same airport within 25 statute miles under a letter of authorization, ferry and training flights, aerial work such as crop dusting, banner towing, survey, aerial photography, firefighting, power line and pipeline patrol and parachute operations, and emergency mail service. These are the jobs a fresh commercial pilot can actually take.
items.reg: 14 CFR Part 119, Subpart A, Section 119.1, Applicability, paragraph (e)
items.why: The direct answer to what a new commercial pilot may be paid to do, so it is asked on essentially every ride.

items.x: Not an acronym.
items.d: A commercial pilot who does not hold an instrument rating in the same category and class is limited by the certificate to not carrying passengers for compensation or hire on cross-country flights of more than 50 nautical miles, or at night. The limitation is placed on the certificate itself. If the applicant holds the instrument rating, the limitation does not appear.
items.reg: 14 CFR Part 61, Subpart F, Section 61.133, Commercial pilot privileges and limitations, paragraph (b)
items.why: A certificate limitation an examiner reads straight off the plastic, and it links privileges to night and weather.

items.x: P - Pilot. I - In. C - Command.
items.d: The pilot in command is the person who has final authority and responsibility for the operation and safety of the flight, has been designated as pilot in command before or during the flight, and holds the appropriate category, class and type rating. The pilot in command is directly responsible for and is the final authority as to the operation of the aircraft and may deviate from any rule to the extent required to meet an in-flight emergency, with a written report on request.
items.reg: 14 CFR Part 1, Section 1.1, General definitions; 14 CFR Part 91, Subpart A, Section 91.3, Responsibility and authority of the pilot in command; 14 CFR Part 61, Subpart A, Section 61.51, Pilot logbooks, paragraph (e)
items.why: The authority behind every airworthiness and go/no-go answer he will ask for.

items.x: Not an acronym.
items.d: Under the private pilot rules a pilot may share the operating expenses of a flight with passengers provided the pilot pays at least a pro rata share, the expenses involve only fuel, oil, airport expenditures or rental fees, and there is a common purpose with a bona fide reason of the pilot's own for making the trip. If any holding out is involved, expense sharing becomes compensation and the flight becomes common carriage. Note that the pro rata rule is a Section 61.113 private pilot provision, not a commercial one.
items.reg: 14 CFR Part 61, Subpart E, Section 61.113, Private pilot privileges and limitations: Pilot in command, paragraph (c); Advisory Circular 61-142, Sharing Aircraft Operating Expenses in Accordance with 14 CFR Section 61.113(c)
items.why: He will test whether you know this belongs to Section 61.113 and not to the commercial privileges section.

items.x: Not an acronym.
items.d: A second class medical certificate is required to exercise commercial pilot privileges and is valid for 12 calendar months regardless of the holder's age, after which it reverts to third class privileges for the remainder of the third class duration. Private pilot privileges require only a third class medical or BasicMed. This is the medical the candidate must be holding on checkride day.
items.reg: 14 CFR Part 61, Subpart A, Section 61.23, Medical certificates: Requirement and duration
items.why: He will check the certificate and ask what class it must be, and it is the applicant's own paperwork.

items.x: Not an acronym.
items.d: Part 91 contains the general operating and flight rules that apply to all civil aircraft operations in the United States unless a more restrictive part applies. Under Part 91 the IFR takeoff minimums do not apply to the pilot, there is no requirement for an operating certificate, and the pilot in command has wide latitude. The candidate's checkride is a Part 91 operation, and every answer should be framed that way unless the examiner changes the scenario.
items.reg: 14 CFR Part 91, Subpart A, Section 91.1, Applicability
items.why: The stated context of this ride, and the baseline against which every carriage scenario is compared.

items.x: L - Letter. O - of. A - Authorization.
items.d: A letter of authorization is an FAA document issued to permit a specific operation, such as nonstop commercial air tours within 25 statute miles of the departure airport under the Section 119.1 paragraph (e) exception. The Gold Seal guide's privileges flowchart refers to it as a letter of approval or letter of authorization. It is not an operating certificate and it does not confer Part 135 authority.
items.reg: 14 CFR Part 119, Subpart A, Section 119.1, Applicability, paragraph (e); 14 CFR Part 136, Subpart A, National Air Tour Safety Standards
items.why: Likely as a follow-up to the air tour exception, but secondary to the exception itself.

items.x: A - Air. T - Taxi. C - Commercial. O - Operator.
items.d: Air taxi and commercial operator is an older term for an operator conducting on-demand passenger or cargo operations for compensation, now largely covered by Part 135 certificate holders. The abbreviation appears on page 31 of the Gold Seal guide's terms list. In current usage you would speak of a Part 135 on-demand operator.
items.reg: 14 CFR Part 119, Subpart A, Section 119.1, Applicability
items.why: On the page 31 list but the modern phrasing is Part 135, so it is unlikely to be asked by name.

items.x: I - Illness. M - Medication. S - Stress. A - Alcohol. F - Fatigue. E - Emotion, and in the Gold Seal guide's version also Eating.
items.d: IM SAFE is the preflight self-assessment a pilot runs before every flight to decide whether he personally is fit to fly. It backs up Section 91.17, which prohibits acting as a crewmember within 8 hours of consuming alcohol, while under the influence, with a blood alcohol concentration of 0.04 percent or greater, or while using any drug that affects faculties contrary to safety. The common variant writes the E as Emotion only; the guide prints Emotion/Eating.
items.reg: 14 CFR Part 91, Subpart A, Section 91.17, Alcohol or drugs; 14 CFR Part 61, Subpart A, Section 61.53, Prohibition on operations during medical deficiency; Aeronautical Information Manual, Paragraph 8-1-1, Fitness for Flight
items.why: A required-item mnemonic that appears in the ACS risk management elements, so it is asked on essentially every ride.

items.x: P - Pilot. A - Aircraft. V - EnVironment. E - External pressures.
items.d: PAVE is the risk assessment checklist used during preflight planning to sort hazards into four categories so none is overlooked. The pilot element folds in IM SAFE, the aircraft element folds in airworthiness and performance, the environment element covers weather, terrain, airport and airspace, and external pressures covers schedule, passengers and get-there-itis. The Gold Seal guide labels this box Preflight General.
items.reg: FAA-H-8083-2, Risk Management Handbook; FAA-S-ACS-7, Commercial Pilot for Airplane Category Airman Certification Standards
items.why: The ACS builds risk management into every task, so he must be able to recite and apply it.

items.x: D - Detect that a change has occurred. E - Estimate the need to counter or react to the change. C - Choose a desirable outcome. I - Identify actions which could successfully control the change. D - Do the necessary action. E - Evaluate the effect of the action.
items.d: The DECIDE model is a continuous loop for in-flight decision making once something changes from the plan. It is deliberately cyclical: the final evaluate step feeds back into detect. You use it to narrate a diversion, an equipment failure or a weather deterioration in a way that shows structured reasoning rather than reaction.
items.reg: FAA-H-8083-2, Risk Management Handbook; FAA-H-8083-25, Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, Chapter 2, Aeronautical Decision-Making
items.why: The named aeronautical decision making model in the handbooks and a routine recite-and-apply item.

items.x: P - Plan. P - Plane. P - Pilot. P - Passengers. P - Programming.
items.d: The 5 Ps is a risk review applied at fixed decision points in the flight: before preflight, before takeoff, at cruise, before descent and before approach. Plan covers the mission, route, weather and fuel; Plane covers mechanical status and fuel state; Pilot covers IM SAFE; Passengers covers their comfort, experience and any pressure they create; Programming covers the avionics and autopilot setup. This mnemonic does not appear in the Gold Seal guide; it comes from the FAA risk management material.
items.reg: FAA-H-8083-2, Risk Management Handbook; FAA-H-8083-16, Instrument Procedures Handbook
items.why: Standard FAA risk model that examiners pair with PAVE, and he asked for it by name.

items.x: A - Aeronautical. D - Decision. M - Making.
items.d: Aeronautical decision making is the systematic approach to the mental process used by pilots to consistently determine the best course of action in response to a given set of circumstances. It encompasses hazard identification, risk assessment, the hazardous attitudes and their antidotes, and the structured models such as DECIDE, PAVE and the 3P model. It is the umbrella heading under which the ACS risk management elements sit.
items.reg: FAA-H-8083-2, Risk Management Handbook; FAA-H-8083-25, Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, Chapter 2, Aeronautical Decision-Making
items.why: Listed on page 31 and it is the heading for an entire ACS area of operation.

items.x: The five are Anti-Authority, Impulsivity, Invulnerability, Macho and Resignation.
items.d: The five hazardous attitudes are the mental states that lead to poor decisions, each with a prescribed antidote: Anti-Authority is countered by follow the rules, they are usually right; Impulsivity by not so fast, think first; Invulnerability by it could happen to me; Macho by taking chances is foolish; and Resignation by I am not helpless, I can make a difference. You are expected to recognize them in a scenario and name the antidote. They do not appear in the Gold Seal guide.
items.reg: FAA-H-8083-2, Risk Management Handbook; FAA-H-8083-25, Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, Chapter 2, Aeronautical Decision-Making
items.why: An ACS risk management element with a fixed list of five and five antidotes, which is exactly what a checkoff examiner wants.

items.x: P - Perceive the given set of circumstances for a flight. P - Process by evaluating their impact on flight safety. P - Perform by implementing the best course of action.
items.d: The 3P model is the practical risk management loop the FAA pairs with PAVE: you perceive hazards using PAVE, process them by asking what could hurt me, my passengers or my aircraft, and perform by mitigating, and then you repeat continuously. It is deliberately simpler than DECIDE so it can be run in flight without a written worksheet. This model does not appear in the Gold Seal guide.
items.reg: FAA-H-8083-2, Risk Management Handbook
items.why: Likely as the mitigation half of a PAVE answer, though DECIDE and PAVE come first.

items.x: S - Single-pilot. R - Resource. M - Management.
items.d: Single-pilot resource management is the art of managing all resources available to a single pilot, inside and outside the cockpit, to ensure a successful flight. It includes ADM, risk management, task management, automation management, controlled flight into terrain awareness and situational awareness. Crew resource management, CRM, is the multi-crew equivalent. Neither term appears in the Gold Seal guide.
items.reg: FAA-H-8083-2, Risk Management Handbook; FAA-S-ACS-7, Commercial Pilot for Airplane Category Airman Certification Standards
items.why: Named in the ACS but usually assessed in flight rather than quizzed on the ground.

items.x: Not an acronym. Also called plan continuation bias.
items.d: Get-there-itis is the external pressure to complete a flight as planned despite deteriorating conditions, and it is the classic External factor in PAVE. For a commercial pilot it is sharper than for a private pilot because a paying customer is waiting. You counter it by setting personal minimums and hard decision points before departure.
items.reg: FAA-H-8083-2, Risk Management Handbook
items.why: Likely in a commercial carriage scenario where a customer is applying pressure.

items.x: Not an acronym.
items.d: Personal minimums are self-imposed limits on weather, currency, fatigue, fuel reserves and airport conditions that are more conservative than the regulations, set in advance and in writing so they are not negotiated in the moment. An examiner will usually ask what yours are and will expect numbers, not generalities. They do not appear in the Gold Seal guide.
items.reg: FAA-H-8083-2, Risk Management Handbook; FAA-S-ACS-7, Commercial Pilot for Airplane Category Airman Certification Standards
items.why: Commonly asked, and the answer must be specific numbers rather than a concept.

items.x: Not an acronym. From the Greek for under-oxygen.
items.d: Hypoxia is a condition of the body in which the tissues are starved of oxygen. The four types are hypoxic, hypemic, stagnant and histotoxic. Symptoms include euphoria, impaired judgment, cyanosis, headache and tunnel vision, and the insidious danger is that judgment degrades before the pilot notices. The Gold Seal guide's solution is to don an oxygen mask if one is available and descend immediately to the lowest practical altitude.
items.reg: 14 CFR Part 91, Subpart C, Section 91.211, Supplemental oxygen; FAA-H-8083-25, Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, Chapter 17, Aeromedical Factors
items.why: A fixed list of four types makes it a checkoff item, and it is in every aeromedical block.

items.x: Not an acronym. Also called altitude hypoxia.
items.d: Hypoxic hypoxia results from insufficient oxygen available to the body as a whole, most commonly because the partial pressure of oxygen falls with altitude. It is the type the supplemental oxygen regulation is written to prevent. The remedy is supplemental oxygen or descent.
items.reg: 14 CFR Part 91, Subpart C, Section 91.211, Supplemental oxygen; FAA-H-8083-25, Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, Chapter 17, Aeromedical Factors
items.why: He asked for the hypoxia types explicitly and this is the one tied to a regulation.

items.x: Not an acronym. Hypemic means deficient in blood.
items.d: Hypemic hypoxia occurs when the blood is not able to take up and transport a sufficient amount of oxygen to the cells, even though enough oxygen is being breathed. Causes include anemia, blood loss and carbon monoxide poisoning, because carbon monoxide binds to hemoglobin far more readily than oxygen does. This is the link between the hypoxia question and the exhaust-shroud cabin heat question.
items.reg: FAA-H-8083-25, Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, Chapter 17, Aeromedical Factors
items.why: It is the bridge from aeromedical straight into his powerplant and exhaust system focus.

items.x: Not an acronym. Stagnant means not flowing.
items.d: Stagnant hypoxia results when the oxygen-rich blood in the lungs is not moving, so oxygen is not delivered to the tissues. Causes include heart failure, shock, a constricted blood vessel and excessive acceleration forces pooling blood away from the brain. Cold temperatures causing vasoconstriction in the extremities is a common general aviation example.
items.reg: FAA-H-8083-25, Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, Chapter 17, Aeromedical Factors
items.why: Part of the four-type recitation he will be asked to complete.

items.x: Not an acronym. Histo means tissue and toxic means poisoned.
items.d: Histotoxic hypoxia is the inability of the cells to effectively use oxygen that is in fact being delivered to them. It is caused by substances that poison cellular respiration, most commonly alcohol and certain drugs, and cyanide in the classic example. It is the one type that supplemental oxygen will not fix.
items.reg: FAA-H-8083-25, Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, Chapter 17, Aeromedical Factors
items.why: Completes the four and is the one that ties back to the alcohol rules.

items.x: Not an acronym. Hyper means excessive and ventilation means breathing.
items.d: Hyperventilation is an excessive rate and depth of respiration leading to an abnormal loss of carbon dioxide from the blood, usually triggered by stress, anxiety or fright. Its symptoms closely resemble those of hypoxia, and the Gold Seal guide correctly advises that when in doubt you treat it as hypoxia and descend. The remedy is to slow the breathing rate, talk aloud, or breathe into a bag to restore carbon dioxide.
items.reg: FAA-H-8083-25, Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, Chapter 17, Aeromedical Factors
items.why: Always paired with hypoxia because the two are deliberately confusable.

items.x: CO is the chemical symbol: C - Carbon. O - Oxygen, one atom.
items.d: Carbon monoxide is a colorless, odorless, tasteless gas produced by the combustion of carbon-based materials, and in a light airplane it reaches the cabin through a crack in the exhaust system feeding the cabin heat muff. It binds to hemoglobin roughly 200 times more readily than oxygen, producing hypemic hypoxia, and symptoms begin with headache, drowsiness and dizziness. The remedy is to turn the cabin heat off, ventilate the cabin, open a window if able, use supplemental oxygen if available and land as soon as possible.
items.reg: FAA-H-8083-25, Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, Chapter 17, Aeromedical Factors; 14 CFR Part 91, Subpart E, Section 91.409, Inspections
items.why: The cabin heat shroud is an exhaust system component, so it sits inside his powerplant focus as well as aeromedical.

items.x: Not an acronym.
items.d: No person may act or attempt to act as a crewmember of a civil aircraft within 8 hours after the consumption of any alcoholic beverage, while under the influence of alcohol, while using any drug that affects the person's faculties in a way contrary to safety, or while having a blood alcohol concentration of 0.04 percent or greater. The Gold Seal guide adds that the body needs about 3 hours to eliminate the alcohol in one drink, so 8 hours is a floor and not a guarantee of fitness.
items.reg: 14 CFR Part 91, Subpart A, Section 91.17, Alcohol or drugs
items.why: A numeric regulation an examiner can check off, and it is the A in IM SAFE.

items.x: Not an acronym.
items.d: A first class medical is required for airline transport pilot privileges and is valid 12 calendar months under age 40 and 6 calendar months at age 40 and over, reverting to lower class privileges thereafter. A second class is required for commercial privileges and is valid 12 calendar months regardless of age, then reverts to third class privileges. A third class covers private pilot, flight instructor and student pilot privileges and is valid 60 calendar months under age 40 and 24 calendar months at age 40 and over.
items.reg: 14 CFR Part 61, Subpart A, Section 61.23, Medical certificates: Requirement and duration
items.why: His own certificate must be a current second class, so this gets verified before the oral starts.

items.x: Not an acronym. It is the common name for the alternative medical qualification.
items.d: BasicMed lets a pilot fly without an FAA medical certificate provided he holds a US driver's license, has held an FAA medical after 14 July 2006, completes a physical with a state-licensed physician using the Comprehensive Medical Examination Checklist, and completes a BasicMed medical education course. The aircraft must be authorized to carry not more than 7 occupants with a maximum certificated takeoff weight not over 12,500 pounds, carrying not more than 6 passengers, at or below 18,000 feet, not exceeding 250 knots, within the United States, and not for compensation or hire. The Gold Seal guide cites Section 91.113 for BasicMed, which is wrong: Section 91.113 is the right-of-way rules; the correct citations are 14 CFR Part 68 and Section 61.113 paragraph (i).
items.reg: 14 CFR Part 68, Requirements for Operating Certain Small Aircraft Without a Medical Certificate; 14 CFR Part 61, Subpart E, Section 61.113, Private pilot privileges and limitations: Pilot in command, paragraph (i)
items.why: Likely as the contrast to the second class medical, and the not-for-hire limit makes the commercial point for him.

items.x: Not an acronym.
items.d: The leans is the most common spatial disorientation illusion. It is caused by a sudden return to level flight following a gradual, prolonged turn that went unnoticed by the vestibular system, so level flight feels like a bank in the opposite direction. The pilot may lean in the direction of the original turn in an attempt to regain the perception of correct vertical posture. The cure is to trust and fly the instruments.
items.reg: FAA-H-8083-25, Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, Chapter 17, Aeromedical Factors; Aeronautical Information Manual, Paragraph 8-1-5, Illusions in Flight
items.why: Likely if he goes to night or instrument scenarios, but outside his four stated focus areas.

items.x: Not an acronym. Named for the Coriolis effect.
items.d: The Coriolis illusion occurs when a pilot has been in a turn long enough for the fluid in the semicircular canals to move at the same speed as the canal, and then moves his head, which sets fluid moving in another canal and creates the overwhelming sensation of turning or accelerating on an entirely different axis. The disoriented pilot may maneuver the aircraft into a dangerous attitude trying to correct. It is considered the most dangerous of the illusions.
items.reg: FAA-H-8083-25, Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, Chapter 17, Aeromedical Factors; Aeronautical Information Manual, Paragraph 8-1-5, Illusions in Flight
items.why: Standard illusion list item, likely only if he works through night or hood scenarios.

items.x: Not an acronym.
items.d: The graveyard spiral occurs in a prolonged coordinated constant-rate turn when the vestibular fluid settles and the pilot stops sensing the turn. On recovering to level flight the pilot feels a turn in the opposite direction, returns the airplane to the original turn, and then responds to the resulting loss of altitude by pulling back, which tightens the spiral and increases the descent rate. Recovery requires leveling the wings by reference to instruments before arresting the descent.
items.reg: FAA-H-8083-25, Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, Chapter 17, Aeromedical Factors; Aeronautical Information Manual, Paragraph 8-1-5, Illusions in Flight
items.why: Likely if he asks about inadvertent VFR into IMC, which is a common commercial scenario.

items.x: Not an acronym. Somato means body and gravic refers to gravity.
items.d: A rapid linear acceleration, such as on takeoff, stimulates the otolith organs in the same way a nose-up pitch would, creating the illusion of a nose-high attitude. The disoriented pilot may push the aircraft into a nose-low or diving attitude, which is lethal on a dark night takeoff over water or unlit terrain. A rapid deceleration produces the opposite illusion of a nose-low attitude.
items.reg: FAA-H-8083-25, Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, Chapter 17, Aeromedical Factors; Aeronautical Information Manual, Paragraph 8-1-5, Illusions in Flight
items.why: The illusion most tied to night takeoffs, which matter for commercial night carriage.

items.x: Not an acronym.
items.d: At cabin pressure altitudes above 12,500 feet MSL up to and including 14,000 feet MSL, the required minimum flight crew must use supplemental oxygen for that part of the flight at those altitudes of more than 30 minutes duration. Above 14,000 feet MSL the required minimum flight crew must use it for the entire flight at those altitudes. Above 15,000 feet MSL each occupant must be provided with supplemental oxygen. All of these are cabin pressure altitudes.
items.reg: 14 CFR Part 91, Subpart C, Section 91.211, Supplemental oxygen
items.why: A clean numeric rule he can check, though the Warrior will rarely see those altitudes.

items.x: Not an acronym.
items.d: Rods in the periphery of the retina provide night vision and take about 30 minutes to fully dark-adapt, while cones in the fovea provide color and detail but are nearly useless at low light, which creates a night blind spot in the center of vision. You therefore use off-center viewing at night, scanning 10 degrees off the object, and you preserve adaptation with red or low white cabin lighting. This is not covered in the Gold Seal guide.
items.reg: FAA-H-8083-25, Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, Chapter 17, Aeromedical Factors; Aeronautical Information Manual, Paragraph 8-1-6, Vision in Flight
items.why: Likely because commercial night carriage is a named privilege limitation.

items.x: Not an acronym.
items.d: An abrupt change from a climb to straight-and-level flight can stimulate the otolith organs enough to create the illusion of tumbling backward. The disoriented pilot may push the aircraft abruptly into a nose-low attitude, which may intensify the illusion.
items.reg: FAA-H-8083-25, Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, Chapter 17, Aeromedical Factors; Aeronautical Information Manual, Paragraph 8-1-5, Illusions in Flight
items.why: On the list but rarely singled out unless he works down the whole illusion set.

items.x: Not an acronym.
items.d: An abrupt upward vertical acceleration, such as in an updraft, stimulates the otolith organs to create the illusion of being in a climb. The disoriented pilot may push the aircraft into a nose-low attitude. A downdraft produces the opposite illusion of descending.
items.reg: FAA-H-8083-25, Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, Chapter 17, Aeromedical Factors; Aeronautical Information Manual, Paragraph 8-1-5, Illusions in Flight
items.why: Completes the vestibular set but is seldom asked on its own.

items.x: Not an acronym.
items.d: The false horizon illusion arises from attempting to align the aircraft with a sloping cloud formation, an obscured horizon, an aurora, a dark scene spread with ground lights and stars, or certain geometric ground patterns. The disoriented pilot may place the aircraft in a dangerous attitude. It is a visual illusion rather than a vestibular one.
items.reg: FAA-H-8083-25, Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, Chapter 17, Aeromedical Factors; Aeronautical Information Manual, Paragraph 8-1-5, Illusions in Flight
items.why: Visual illusion, possible in a night scenario but not a focus area.

items.x: Not an acronym. Auto means self and kinesis means movement.
items.d: Autokinesis occurs at night when a single stationary light stared at for several seconds appears to move. The disoriented pilot may attempt to align the aircraft with the perceived moving light and lose control. The remedy is to avoid fixating and to keep the eyes scanning.
items.reg: FAA-H-8083-25, Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, Chapter 17, Aeromedical Factors; Aeronautical Information Manual, Paragraph 8-1-5, Illusions in Flight
items.why: Classic night illusion, possible but not central to a systems-focused ride.

items.x: A - Aviation. M - Medical. E - Examiner.
items.d: An aviation medical examiner is a physician designated by the FAA to perform medical examinations and issue medical certificates. You deal with one for the second class medical required for commercial privileges. The term is listed on page 31 of the Gold Seal guide.
items.reg: 14 CFR Part 61, Subpart A, Section 61.23, Medical certificates: Requirement and duration; 14 CFR Part 67, Medical Standards and Certification
