items.why: On the page 31 list but it is vocabulary rather than a question.

items.x: M - Meteorological. E - Terminal. A - Aviation. R - Report. The FAA expands it as Aviation Routine Weather Report, from the French message d'observation meteorologique regulier pour l'aviation.
items.d: A METAR is a routine surface observation that gives a snapshot in time of weather at a terminal, issued hourly, normally between 55 and 59 minutes past the hour. The elements run in fixed order: station identifier, date and time in Zulu, wind, visibility, present weather, sky condition, temperature and dew point in Celsius, altimeter setting in inches of mercury, and remarks. A SPECI is the unscheduled special observation issued when conditions change significantly.
items.reg: Aeronautical Information Manual, Paragraph 7-1-29, Key to Aviation Routine Weather Report (METAR) and Aerodrome Forecasts (TAF); Advisory Circular 00-45, Aviation Weather Services
items.why: Every commercial oral has the applicant read a live METAR aloud.

items.x: T - Terminal. A - Aerodrome. F - Forecast.
items.d: A terminal aerodrome forecast gives expected conditions within 5 statute miles of an airport, issued at least four times a day and valid for a 24 or 30 hour period. Change groups include FM for a rapid from-group change, TEMPO for temporary conditions expected less than half the period and lasting less than an hour at a time, BECMG for a gradual change, and PROB for a probability group. The TAF drives the Section 91.169 alternate decision.
items.reg: Aeronautical Information Manual, Paragraph 7-1-29, Key to Aviation Routine Weather Report (METAR) and Aerodrome Forecasts (TAF); 14 CFR Part 91, Subpart B, Section 91.169, IFR flight plan: Information required
items.why: Paired with the METAR in the weather walk and it feeds the alternate rule.

items.x: PI - Pilot. REP - Report. The full name is Pilot Weather Report.
items.d: A pilot report is an observation of actual conditions aloft filed by a pilot, coded UA for routine and UUA for urgent. It is the only direct observation of turbulence, icing, cloud tops and in-flight visibility, so it is the most valuable product for deciding whether a forecast is holding. You are expected to say that you will file one, particularly for icing or turbulence.
items.reg: Aeronautical Information Manual, Paragraph 7-1-19, Pilot Weather Reports (PIREPs); Advisory Circular 00-45, Aviation Weather Services
items.why: Examiners reliably ask what you would do after encountering unforecast conditions, and filing a PIREP is the answer.

items.x: AIR - Airmen's. MET - Meteorological Information. Formally the Airmen's Meteorological Information advisory, also called a WA.
items.d: An AIRMET advises of weather hazardous to aircraft with limited capability, affecting an area of at least 3,000 square miles, valid 6 hours. Sierra covers mountain obscuration and instrument flight rules conditions, Tango covers moderate turbulence and sustained surface winds of 30 knots or more and low-level wind shear, and Zulu covers moderate icing and freezing levels. These are the advisories that most directly limit a Warrior.
items.reg: Aeronautical Information Manual, Paragraph 7-1-6, Inflight Aviation Weather Advisories; Advisory Circular 00-45, Aviation Weather Services
items.why: Listed on page 31 and it is the advisory that governs go/no-go for a light single.

items.x: SIG - Significant. MET - Meteorological Information. Formally Significant Meteorological Information, also called a WS.
items.d: A SIGMET advises of weather significant to the safety of all aircraft, affecting at least 3,000 square miles, valid 4 hours, covering severe icing not associated with thunderstorms, severe or extreme turbulence or clear air turbulence not associated with thunderstorms, dust storms or sandstorms lowering visibility below 3 miles, and volcanic ash. A Convective SIGMET, issued hourly and valid 2 hours, covers embedded or lines of thunderstorms, severe thunderstorms and tornadoes, and it implies severe turbulence, severe icing and low-level wind shear.
items.reg: Aeronautical Information Manual, Paragraph 7-1-6, Inflight Aviation Weather Advisories; Advisory Circular 00-45, Aviation Weather Services
items.why: Listed on page 32 and the contrast with AIRMET is a near-certain question.

items.x: Not an acronym.
items.d: The closer the temperature and dew point, the higher the relative humidity and the greater the likelihood of fog, low ceilings and visible moisture. A spread of 4 degrees Celsius or less and narrowing is the usual warning sign for fog formation. The same figures tell you about carburetor icing risk, which can occur at ambient temperatures as high as the low 30s Celsius with sufficient humidity.
items.reg: FAA-H-8083-25, Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, Chapter 13, Weather Theory; Special Airworthiness Information Bulletin CE-09-35, Carburetor Icing Prevention
items.why: It is the one weather figure that feeds directly into his carburetor icing line of questions.

items.x: 1 - From 1 hour before to 1 hour after the estimated time of arrival. 2 - Ceiling at least 2,000 feet above airport elevation. 3 - Visibility at least 3 statute miles.
items.d: An alternate airport must be filed on an IFR flight plan unless the destination has at least one instrument approach procedure and, for the period from 1 hour before to 1 hour after the estimated time of arrival, the forecast ceiling is at least 2,000 feet above the airport elevation and the forecast visibility is at least 3 statute miles. The commonly heard variant is the 3-2-1 rule or the 1-2-3 rule stated in either order; the Gold Seal guide prints 1-2-3. Standard alternate minimums are then 600 feet and 2 statute miles for a precision approach and 800 feet and 2 statute miles for a nonprecision approach.
items.reg: 14 CFR Part 91, Subpart B, Section 91.169, IFR flight plan: Information required
items.why: A clean numeric rule, likely if he has the instrument rating, but this is a single-engine land commercial ride under Part 91.

items.x: Not an acronym.
items.d: Rime ice is rough, milky, opaque ice formed by the instantaneous or very rapid freezing of small supercooled droplets as they strike the leading edges, which traps air in the ice. It is lighter than clear ice but its rough surface decreases aerodynamic efficiency. It typically forms in stratiform clouds at colder temperatures.
items.reg: Aeronautical Information Manual, Paragraph 7-1-20, Pilot Weather Reports; FAA-H-8083-25, Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, Chapter 13, Weather Theory
items.why: Likely in the winter-weather block, and the Warrior has no ice protection so the answer is always avoid.

items.x: Not an acronym. Also called glaze ice.
items.d: Clear ice is glossy, transparent ice formed by the relatively slow freezing of large supercooled water droplets, which flow back before freezing. It is denser, harder and heavier than rime ice and much harder to remove. It typically forms in cumuliform clouds and in freezing rain, and it is the most dangerous airframe icing for a light airplane.
items.reg: Aeronautical Information Manual, Paragraph 7-1-20, Pilot Weather Reports; FAA-H-8083-25, Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, Chapter 13, Weather Theory
items.why: Paired with rime in the icing question.

items.x: Not an acronym. The three are cumulus, mature and dissipating.
items.d: In the cumulus stage air warmer than its environment rises, cools and condenses, producing strong updrafts and supercooled water above the freezing level. The mature stage, which begins when precipitation reaches the surface, is characterized by both updrafts and downdrafts, evaporative cooling, outflow when the downdraft spreads at the ground, the anvil top, hail and intense cloud-to-ground lightning. In the dissipating stage downdrafts predominate, the anvil weakens and the cell rains itself out.
items.reg: FAA-H-8083-25, Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, Chapter 13, Weather Theory; Aeronautical Information Manual, Paragraph 7-1-26, Thunderstorms
items.why: A fixed three-item list that examiners use to test thunderstorm avoidance reasoning.

items.x: Not an acronym.
items.d: A microburst is a localized, intense downdraft within a thunderstorm, usually 2.5 statute miles or less in diameter, with winds that can reach 100 miles per hour and a lifespan of around 15 minutes. An airplane entering one meets an increasing headwind, then a strong downdraft, then a sudden tailwind as it exits, which can exceed the climb performance of a light single. The answer is total avoidance.
items.reg: Aeronautical Information Manual, Paragraph 7-1-24, Microbursts; FAA-H-8083-25, Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, Chapter 13, Weather Theory
items.why: A standard low-level windshear scenario, likely if he works a summer-afternoon departure.

items.x: Not an acronym.
items.d: Wind shear is a change in wind speed, wind direction, or both, over a short distance, which produces an abrupt headwind or tailwind change and alters the flight path. It is most dangerous at low levels near the ground, where there is no altitude to trade. Sources include thunderstorms, frontal zones, temperature inversions and strong surface winds past obstructions.
items.reg: Aeronautical Information Manual, Paragraph 7-1-23, Wind Shear; FAA-H-8083-25, Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, Chapter 13, Weather Theory
items.why: Appears in TAFs as a WS group and in the airport environment discussion.

items.x: M - Marginal. V - Visual. F - Flight. R - Rules.
items.d: Marginal visual flight rules describes a ceiling of 1,000 to 3,000 feet inclusive and visibility of 3 to 5 statute miles inclusive. The categories run low IFR below 500 feet or less than 1 mile, IFR 500 to below 1,000 feet or 1 to less than 3 miles, MVFR, and VFR above 3,000 feet and greater than 5 miles. These are flight category labels used in briefings and on graphical products, not regulatory minimums.
items.reg: Advisory Circular 00-45, Aviation Weather Services; 14 CFR Part 91, Subpart B, Section 91.155, Basic VFR weather minimums
items.why: Listed on page 31 and it is how he will phrase a borderline go/no-go scenario.

items.x: I - International. S - Standard. A - Atmosphere.
items.d: The international standard atmosphere is the reference condition of 15 degrees Celsius and 29.92 inches of mercury at sea level, with a temperature lapse rate of 2 degrees Celsius per 1,000 feet and a pressure lapse of approximately 1 inch of mercury per 1,000 feet. All performance charts are built against it, so you correct for the difference between actual and standard conditions to get density altitude. Expect to be asked for the standard temperature at a given altitude.
items.reg: FAA-H-8083-25, Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, Chapter 4, Principles of Flight; 14 CFR Part 91, Subpart B, Section 91.121, Altimeter settings
items.why: Listed on page 31 and it underpins every performance chart he will make you run.

items.x: O - Outside. A - Air. T - Temperature.
items.d: Outside air temperature is the free air temperature at the aircraft, read from the cockpit gauge and used as the entry argument for density altitude, true airspeed and performance chart corrections. It is also the number you compare against the dew point to anticipate carburetor icing and visible moisture.
items.reg: FAA-H-8083-25, Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, Chapter 11, Aircraft Performance
items.why: Listed on page 31 and it is the chart input for the performance problems he will set.

items.x: Hg is the chemical symbol for mercury, from the Latin hydrargyrum.
items.d: Inches of mercury is the unit of the altimeter setting and of manifold pressure in the United States. Standard sea level pressure is 29.92 inches of mercury. An altimeter set to a pressure lower than actual reads low, and flying from high pressure to low pressure without resetting makes the altimeter over-read, which is the origin of the phrase high to low, look out below.
items.reg: 14 CFR Part 91, Subpart B, Section 91.121, Altimeter settings
items.why: Listed on page 31 and it is the unit behind the altimeter setting question.

items.x: G - Graphical. F - Forecast. A - for Aviation.
items.d: The Graphical Forecast for Aviation is the web-based set of observation and forecast maps that replaced the textual area forecast for the contiguous United States, covering clouds, visibility, precipitation, icing, turbulence and winds aloft from 14 hours in the past to 18 hours ahead. It is the product you actually use for a cross-country briefing today. It is not listed in the Gold Seal guide.
items.reg: Advisory Circular 00-45, Aviation Weather Services
items.why: The live replacement for a product the guide still lists, which is exactly the gap an examiner probes.

items.x: Not an acronym. The codes combine an intensity sign, a descriptor, and a precipitation or obscuration code.
items.d: Intensity is shown by a minus sign for light, no sign for moderate and a plus sign for heavy. Descriptors include MI shallow, BL blowing, BC patches, SH showers, PR partial, DR drifting, TS thunderstorm and FZ freezing. Precipitation codes include DZ drizzle, RA rain, SN snow, PL ice pellets, GR hail, GS small hail or snow pellets, SG snow grains and IC ice crystals. Obscurations include BR mist, FG fog, HZ haze, FU smoke, SA sand, DU widespread dust, PY spray and VA volcanic ash.
items.reg: Aeronautical Information Manual, Paragraph 7-1-29, Key to Aviation Routine Weather Report (METAR) and Aerodrome Forecasts (TAF)
items.why: He will hand over a real METAR and expect the codes decoded without a legend.

items.x: Not an acronym.
items.d: Radiation fog forms on clear, calm nights as the ground cools by radiation and chills the air to its dew point. Advection fog forms when warm moist air moves over a cooler surface and requires wind. Upslope fog forms as moist stable air is lifted and cooled adiabatically. Steam fog forms when cold dry air moves over warm water. Precipitation-induced fog forms when warm rain falls through cooler air. Fog types are not covered in the Gold Seal guide.
items.reg: FAA-H-8083-25, Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, Chapter 13, Weather Theory
items.why: A standard weather block question and a gap in the guide he may land on.

items.x: Not an acronym.
items.d: Mixed ice is a combination of clear and rime ice, formed when droplets of varying size are present. Its roughness and weight both affect aerodynamics. It is the most commonly reported icing type in practice.
items.reg: Aeronautical Information Manual, Paragraph 7-1-20, Pilot Weather Reports; FAA-H-8083-25, Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, Chapter 13, Weather Theory
items.why: Completes the icing set but is seldom asked on its own.

items.x: Not an acronym. The four are trace, light, moderate and severe.
items.d: Trace icing is perceptible but not hazardous unless encountered for an extended period. Light icing is clearly visible and anti-icing or deicing equipment removes or prevents accumulation. Moderate icing means even short encounters can be hazardous and anti-icing or deicing equipment must be used or a diversion made. Severe icing means the rate of accumulation is such that deicing and anti-icing equipment fails to reduce the hazard and diversion is mandatory.
items.reg: Aeronautical Information Manual, Paragraph 7-1-20, Pilot Weather Reports; Advisory Circular 00-45, Aviation Weather Services
items.why: Reporting vocabulary rather than a decision rule for an airplane with no ice protection.

items.x: C - Clear. A - Air. T - Turbulence.
items.d: Clear air turbulence is turbulence occurring outside of convective clouds, typically associated with the jet stream, wind shear at high altitude and mountain waves. It is reported in SIGMETs when severe. It is largely a high-altitude concern and not a routine factor for a Warrior.
items.reg: Aeronautical Information Manual, Paragraph 7-1-22, Turbulence; Advisory Circular 00-45, Aviation Weather Services
items.why: On the page 31 list but outside the operating envelope of this airplane.

items.x: M - Milli. B - Bar. A millibar, equivalent to a hectopascal.
items.d: The millibar is the pressure unit used on surface analysis charts and in the sea level pressure remark in a METAR, where SLP127 means 1012.7 hectopascals. One inch of mercury is approximately 33.86 millibars. Outside the United States altimeter settings are given in hectopascals.
items.reg: Advisory Circular 00-45, Aviation Weather Services
items.why: On the page 31 list and only relevant when decoding the sea level pressure remark.

items.x: F - Forecast. A - Area. The product is the Area Forecast.
items.d: The area forecast was a text forecast of general weather conditions over an area the size of several states, used to determine en route and destination weather where no TAF existed. It has been discontinued for the contiguous United States and replaced by the Graphical Forecast for Aviation. The Gold Seal guide still lists it on page 31 without noting that it is retired.
items.reg: Advisory Circular 00-45, Aviation Weather Services
items.why: On the page 31 list but a retired product, so it only comes up as a history question.

items.x: S - Radar. D - Weather Report. The guide gives SD as Radar Weather Report.
items.d: SD was the identifier for the textual radar weather report, which described precipitation echo type, intensity, coverage and movement. These textual radar reports have been discontinued and replaced by graphical radar imagery. The Gold Seal guide lists it on page 32 without noting its retirement, and the letters SD are a product identifier rather than an expandable acronym.
items.reg: Advisory Circular 00-45, Aviation Weather Services
items.why: A retired textual product listed on page 32 for completeness only.

items.x: T - Transcribed. W - Weather. E - En route. B - Broadcast.
items.d: The transcribed weather en route broadcast was a continuous recorded weather and aeronautical information broadcast over selected navigational aids. It has been discontinued in the contiguous United States. It appears on page 32 of the Gold Seal guide.
items.reg: Aeronautical Information Manual, Paragraph 7-1-9, Flight Service Weather Products
items.why: A retired service on the page 32 list, included only for completeness.

items.x: T - Telephone. I - Information. B - Briefing. S - Service.
items.d: The telephone information briefing service was an automated recorded telephone briefing of area and route weather. It has been discontinued. It appears on page 32 of the Gold Seal guide.
items.reg: Aeronautical Information Manual, Paragraph 7-1-9, Flight Service Weather Products
items.why: A retired service on the page 32 list, included only for completeness.

items.x: AWS: A - Aviation. W - Weather. S - Service. AVW: A - Aviation. V and W - Weather.
items.d: Aviation Weather Service is the umbrella term for the weather products and services provided jointly by the National Weather Service and the FAA, and AVW is the Gold Seal guide's abbreviation for aviation weather generally. Both are listed on page 31 as general vocabulary rather than as specific products you would request.
items.reg: Advisory Circular 00-45, Aviation Weather Services
items.why: Generic page 31 vocabulary with no question attached to it.

items.x: W - Weather. F - Forecast. O - Office.
items.d: A weather forecast office is a National Weather Service field office responsible for forecasts and warnings in its area. It appears on page 32 of the Gold Seal guide as general vocabulary.
items.reg: Advisory Circular 00-45, Aviation Weather Services
items.why: Page 32 vocabulary, not an operational item.

items.x: Not an acronym.
items.d: Density altitude is pressure altitude corrected for nonstandard temperature, and it is the altitude the airplane feels. High density altitude reduces engine power, propeller thrust and wing lift simultaneously, lengthening takeoff and landing distances and flattening climb. You compute it from pressure altitude and outside air temperature, and it is the governing number for every performance chart.
items.reg: FAA-H-8083-25, Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, Chapter 11, Aircraft Performance; 14 CFR Part 91, Subpart B, Section 91.103, Preflight action
items.why: It ties performance directly to engine power output, which is his focus, and it is asked on every ride.

items.x: Not an acronym.
items.d: Pressure altitude is the altitude indicated when the altimeter is set to 29.92 inches of mercury, that is, altitude corrected for nonstandard pressure. It is the entry argument for performance charts and the altitude reference above 18,000 feet MSL. You obtain it by setting 29.92 in the Kollsman window or by computing it from field elevation and the altimeter setting.
items.reg: FAA-H-8083-25, Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, Chapter 11, Aircraft Performance; 14 CFR Part 91, Subpart B, Section 91.121, Altimeter settings
items.why: Required before any density altitude or performance answer.

items.x: IAS: I - Indicated. A - Air. S - Speed. CAS: C - Calibrated. EAS: E - Equivalent. TAS: T - True.
items.d: Indicated airspeed is what the airspeed indicator shows. Calibrated airspeed is indicated airspeed corrected for instrument and position error. Equivalent airspeed is calibrated airspeed corrected for compressibility error. True airspeed is the actual speed through the air, equivalent airspeed corrected for nonstandard temperature and pressure. Groundspeed is true airspeed corrected for wind. The Warrior II POH publishes both KIAS and KCAS columns for its airspeed limitations.
items.reg: FAA-H-8083-25, Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, Chapter 8, Flight Instruments; 14 CFR Part 91, Subpart A, Section 91.9, Civil aircraft flight manual, marking, and placard requirements
items.why: A four-step recitation an examiner can check, and the POH prints both columns so he can point at them.

items.x: C - Center. G - of Gravity.
items.d: The center of gravity is the point at which the airplane would balance if suspended, and it must stay within the forward and rearward limits published in the POH for the loaded weight. A forward center of gravity gives higher stall speed, higher required elevator force, slower cruise and more stability, while an aft center of gravity gives lower stall speed and faster cruise but reduced longitudinal stability and a more difficult stall and spin recovery. The Warrior II POH, Piper Report VB-1180, publishes normal category limits of 88.3 to 93.0 inches aft of datum at 2440 pounds; confirm in this airplane's POH.
items.reg: 14 CFR Part 91, Subpart A, Section 91.9, Civil aircraft flight manual, marking, and placard requirements; 14 CFR Part 91, Subpart B, Section 91.103, Preflight action; FAA-H-8083-1, Aircraft Weight and Balance Handbook
items.why: Weight and balance is computed on every ride and the effects of a forward or aft center of gravity are a certain question.

items.x: Not an acronym.
items.d: The Warrior II POH, Piper Report VB-1180, gives a maximum weight of 2440 pounds in the normal category and 2020 pounds in the utility category, a maximum ramp weight of 2447 and 2027 pounds respectively, and maximum baggage of 200 pounds in normal category and zero in utility. Flight load factors are 3.8 G positive in normal category and 4.4 G positive in utility, with no inverted maneuvers approved. Confirm every figure in this airplane's POH, since serial 28-8116257 is covered by the earlier Piper Report VB-880.
items.reg: 14 CFR Part 91, Subpart A, Section 91.9, Civil aircraft flight manual, marking, and placard requirements; FAA-H-8083-1, Aircraft Weight and Balance Handbook
items.why: The commercial maneuvers must be flown in the utility category, so the weight limit decides whether the flight is legal.

items.x: Not an acronym.
items.d: The Warrior II must be operated as a normal or utility category airplane. The POH, Piper Report VB-1180, prohibits all acrobatic maneuvers including spins in the normal category, and approves steep turns, lazy eights and chandelles in the utility category at an entry speed of 111 KIAS with bank angles exceeding 60 degrees. The utility category weight limit of 2020 pounds and the zero baggage allowance are therefore part of planning a commercial maneuvers flight. Confirm in this airplane's POH.
items.reg: 14 CFR Part 91, Subpart A, Section 91.9, Civil aircraft flight manual, marking, and placard requirements; 14 CFR Part 91, Subpart B, Section 91.303, Aerobatic flight
items.why: It is the direct intersection of his airplane's limitations with the commercial maneuvers he must fly.

items.x: Not an acronym.
items.d: Indicated altitude is the uncorrected altitude read from the altimeter with the current setting in the window. True altitude is the actual height above mean sea level, which is what airport and obstacle elevations are published as. Absolute altitude is the height above ground level. Indicated equals true only under standard conditions.
items.reg: FAA-H-8083-25, Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, Chapter 8, Flight Instruments
items.why: Standard altimetry vocabulary, likely as a quick definitions sweep.

items.x: L - Lift. D - Drag. The ratio of lift to drag, and its maximum value.
items.d: The lift-to-drag ratio expresses aerodynamic efficiency, and L over D max is the angle of attack at which lift is greatest relative to drag. L over D max gives the maximum glide range and corresponds to best glide speed, and it is also the point of minimum total drag where parasite and induced drag are equal. It is the aerodynamic basis for the steep spiral and for any engine-out glide.
items.reg: FAA-H-8083-25, Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, Chapter 5, Aerodynamics of Flight
items.why: Listed on page 31 and it is the theory behind the glide and steep spiral answers.

items.x: Not an acronym.
items.d: Unless otherwise authorized, no person may operate an aircraft below 10,000 feet MSL at an indicated airspeed of more than 250 knots, at or below 2,500 feet AGL within 4 nautical miles of the primary airport of Class C or Class D airspace at more than 200 knots, or in the airspace underlying Class B or in a VFR corridor through Class B at more than 200 knots. No person may operate at or above 10,000 feet MSL at more than Mach 1. None of these constrain a Warrior, but the rule is a standard recitation.
items.reg: 14 CFR Part 91, Subpart B, Section 91.117, Aircraft speed
items.why: A clean numeric rule from page 7 of the guide that examiners use as a warm-up.

items.x: NM: N - Nautical. M - Mile. SM: S - Statute. M - Mile.
items.d: A nautical mile is 6,076 feet, one minute of latitude, and is the unit of distance for navigation, airspeed in knots and the 50 nautical mile limit in Section 61.133 paragraph (b). A statute mile is 5,280 feet and is the unit for visibility in METARs, TAFs and the VFR weather minimums. Mixing the two is a classic error in the alternate and visibility rules.
items.reg: 14 CFR Part 91, Subpart B, Section 91.155, Basic VFR weather minimums; 14 CFR Part 61, Subpart F, Section 61.133, Commercial pilot privileges and limitations
items.why: Listed on pages 31 and 32, and the unit distinction matters inside the commercial 50 nautical mile limitation.

items.x: T - True. A - Air. S - Speed.
items.d: True airspeed is the actual speed of the airplane through the air mass, equal to equivalent airspeed corrected for nonstandard temperature and pressure. It increases roughly 2 percent per 1,000 feet above indicated airspeed for a given indication. You compute it for flight planning and for the required reporting of a 5 percent or 10 knot change in cruise true airspeed on an IFR flight plan.
items.reg: FAA-H-8083-25, Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, Chapter 8, Flight Instruments; 14 CFR Part 91, Subpart B, Section 91.183, IFR communications
items.why: Listed on page 32 and used in every flight plan and cruise performance problem.

items.x: Not an acronym. Mach is named for the physicist Ernst Mach.
items.d: The Mach number is the ratio of true airspeed to the local speed of sound. Critical Mach is the lowest Mach number at which airflow over any part of the aircraft first reaches the speed of sound. Neither is a practical concern in a Warrior, but both appear in the Gold Seal guide's speed review on page 7.
items.reg: FAA-H-8083-25, Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, Chapter 5, Aerodynamics of Flight
items.why: In the guide for completeness but has no bearing on a Warrior commercial ride.

items.x: Not an acronym. The word is French for candle.
items.d: A chandelle is a maximum performance 180 degree climbing turn that begins from approximately straight-and-level flight and ends in a wings-level, nose-high attitude just above stall speed. You establish approximately 30 degrees of bank, apply pitch and power together for the first 90 degrees at constant bank with increasing pitch, then begin a constant-rate rollout over the second 90 degrees while holding a constant pitch attitude so airspeed decays to just above a stall at the 180 degree point. ACS tolerances are a rollout heading within plus or minus 10 degrees and completion no lower than 1,500 feet AGL.
items.reg: FAA-S-ACS-7, Commercial Pilot for Airplane Category Airman Certification Standards, Area of Operation VII, Performance Maneuvers and Ground Reference Maneuvers; FAA-H-8083-3, Airplane Flying Handbook, Chapter 10
items.why: One of the four named commercial maneuvers and the oral briefing for it is part of the ride.

items.x: Not an acronym.
items.d: A lazy eight is two 180 degree turns in opposite directions with a continuously changing pitch, bank and airspeed, tracing a lazy figure eight against the horizon. Power is set for an airspeed at or below maneuvering speed, the climbing turn begins toward the 45 degree point, pitch decreases and bank increases to a maximum of approximately 30 degrees and slowest airspeed at the 90 degree point, the bank rolls out while the nose reaches its lowest pitch near the 135 degree point, and the airplane arrives at the 180 degree point straight and level on the original altitude and airspeed. ACS tolerances at the 180 degree point are altitude within 100 feet, airspeed within 10 knots and heading within 10 degrees, no lower than 1,500 feet AGL.
items.reg: FAA-S-ACS-7, Commercial Pilot for Airplane Category Airman Certification Standards, Area of Operation VII, Performance Maneuvers and Ground Reference Maneuvers; FAA-H-8083-3, Airplane Flying Handbook, Chapter 10
items.why: One of the four named commercial maneuvers with specific tolerances he will ask you to state.

items.x: Not an acronym.
items.d: A steep spiral is a gliding turn of at least three complete 360 degree turns at a constant radius around a ground reference point, flown at idle power and best glide airspeed with the bank adjusted for wind drift. It demonstrates the pilot's ability to manage a power-off descent over a chosen point, which is the core skill behind a forced landing. ACS tolerances are a maximum bank of 60 degrees, airspeed within 10 knots of the specified value and completion no lower than 1,500 feet AGL.
items.reg: FAA-S-ACS-7, Commercial Pilot for Airplane Category Airman Certification Standards, Area of Operation VII, Performance Maneuvers and Ground Reference Maneuvers; FAA-H-8083-3, Airplane Flying Handbook, Chapter 10
items.why: A named commercial maneuver flown at best glide, so it feeds straight into his engine failure questions.

items.x: Not an acronym. Also called pylon eights.
items.d: Eights on pylons is the only ground reference maneuver flown at a specific altitude rather than a specific bank: you hold the lateral line of sight reference on the pylon by varying altitude to match the pivotal altitude as groundspeed changes. You enter downwind at a 45 degree angle between the pylons, roll into 30 to 40 degrees of bank abeam the first pylon, climb or descend to keep the wingtip reference on the pylon, then repeat on the opposite pylon. ACS tolerances cap bank at 40 degrees and require the line-of-sight reference to stay on the pylon.
items.reg: FAA-S-ACS-7, Commercial Pilot for Airplane Category Airman Certification Standards, Area of Operation VII, Performance Maneuvers and Ground Reference Maneuvers; FAA-H-8083-3, Airplane Flying Handbook, Chapter 10
items.why: A named commercial maneuver whose theory he will make you derive at the table.

items.x: Not an acronym.
items.d: Pivotal altitude is the altitude at which the aircraft's lateral line of sight extended from the wingtip appears to pivot on a ground point, and it depends only on groundspeed, not on bank angle or wind. The Gold Seal guide gives the formula as groundspeed squared divided by 11.3, plus the MSL elevation of the ground reference, with groundspeed in knots. Because groundspeed changes around the circle, the pivotal altitude changes continuously, which is why eights on pylons requires climbing and descending.
items.reg: FAA-S-ACS-7, Commercial Pilot for Airplane Category Airman Certification Standards, Area of Operation VII, Performance Maneuvers and Ground Reference Maneuvers; FAA-H-8083-3, Airplane Flying Handbook, Chapter 10
items.why: A formula he must produce from memory before being allowed to fly the pylons.

items.t: Power-Off 180 Degree Accuracy Approach and Landing
items.x: Not an acronym.
items.d: This is the commercial landing task in which the engine is brought to idle abeam the intended touchdown point on downwind and the airplane is landed within a specified distance beyond a designated point without adding power. It tests energy management, glide judgment and the use of flaps and slips as drag devices. It is a required ACS task that the Gold Seal guide does not cover in its maneuvers pages.
items.reg: FAA-S-ACS-7, Commercial Pilot for Airplane Category Airman Certification Standards, Area of Operation IV, Takeoffs, Landings, and Go-Arounds; FAA-H-8083-3, Airplane Flying Handbook, Chapter 9
items.why: A required commercial task the guide omits entirely, and it is the landing most applicants are briefed hardest on.

items.x: Not an acronym.
items.d: A steep turn at the commercial level is a 360 or 720 degree turn at 50 degrees of bank, holding altitude, airspeed and bank while managing the load factor and the increase in stall speed. The Warrior II POH approves steep turns in the utility category for bank angles exceeding 60 degrees at an entry speed of 111 KIAS. The oral usually covers load factor, the increase in stall speed with the square root of the load factor, and overbanking tendency.
items.reg: FAA-S-ACS-7, Commercial Pilot for Airplane Category Airman Certification Standards, Area of Operation VII, Performance Maneuvers and Ground Reference Maneuvers; 14 CFR Part 91, Subpart A, Section 91.9, Civil aircraft flight manual, marking, and placard requirements
items.why: Flown on every commercial ride and the load factor discussion is a reliable oral question.

items.x: Not an acronym.
items.d: An accelerated stall occurs when the critical angle of attack is exceeded at a speed higher than the unaccelerated stall speed, because load factor is increased by a turn or an abrupt pull. Stall speed increases with the square root of the load factor, so at 60 degrees of bank with a load factor of 2 the stall speed is about 1.41 times the wings-level figure. This is the risk that sits inside chandelles, lazy eights and steep turns.
items.reg: FAA-S-ACS-7, Commercial Pilot for Airplane Category Airman Certification Standards, Area of Operation VII; FAA-H-8083-3, Airplane Flying Handbook, Chapter 4
items.why: Likely as the risk management element attached to the performance maneuvers.

items.x: Not an acronym. The phases are entry, incipient, developed and recovery, and the recovery acronym is PARE: P - Power idle. A - Ailerons neutral. R - Rudder full opposite. E - Elevator forward.
items.d: A spin is an aggravated stall in which one wing is more stalled than the other, producing autorotation. The Warrior II POH prohibits all acrobatic maneuvers including spins in the normal category and publishes a spin recovery procedure in Section 3. PARE is a widely taught recovery mnemonic that does not appear in the Gold Seal guide, and the POH procedure for the specific airplane always takes precedence over any generic mnemonic.
items.reg: 14 CFR Part 91, Subpart B, Section 91.303, Aerobatic flight; 14 CFR Part 91, Subpart A, Section 91.9, Civil aircraft flight manual, marking, and placard requirements; FAA-H-8083-3, Airplane Flying Handbook, Chapter 4
items.why: Likely as a knowledge item attached to the maneuvers, but spins are not demonstrated on a commercial airplane ride.

items.x: Not an acronym.
items.d: A stall is a rapid decrease in lift caused by the separation of airflow from the wing surface, brought on by exceeding the critical angle of attack. It can occur at any pitch attitude and any airspeed. The Gold Seal guide names three situations in which the critical angle of attack is most commonly exceeded: low speed, high speed with an abrupt change in angle of attack, and turning flight where centrifugal force adds to weight and the required angle of attack rises with bank.
items.reg: FAA-H-8083-25, Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, Chapter 5, Aerodynamics of Flight; FAA-H-8083-3, Airplane Flying Handbook, Chapter 4
items.why: The definition must include critical angle of attack and any attitude or airspeed, and examiners listen for exactly that.

items.x: Not an acronym. Expressed in G, the ratio of load supported to the actual weight.
items.d: Load factor is the ratio of the load supported by the wings to the actual weight of the airplane, and in a level turn it rises with bank angle regardless of airspeed or weight. At 60 degrees of bank the load factor is 2 G. Stall speed increases with the square root of the load factor. The Warrior II POH, Piper Report VB-1180, gives maximum positive load factors of 3.8 G in normal category and 4.4 G in utility category with no inverted maneuvers approved.
items.reg: 14 CFR Part 91, Subpart A, Section 91.9, Civil aircraft flight manual, marking, and placard requirements; FAA-H-8083-25, Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, Chapter 5, Aerodynamics of Flight
items.why: It links the POH limitations to the steep turns and chandelles he will watch you fly.

items.x: Not an acronym.
items.d: Parasite drag is drag produced by the motion of an object through a fluid, made up of form drag, skin friction and interference drag, and it increases with the square of airspeed. Induced drag arises from the production of lift and decreases as airspeed increases. The two curves cross at L over D max, which is the speed of minimum total drag and therefore best glide and best endurance in a jet. Ground effect reduces induced drag by interfering with the formation of wingtip vortices.
items.reg: FAA-H-8083-25, Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, Chapter 5, Aerodynamics of Flight
items.why: Standard aerodynamics, likely as the theory behind the glide and best-speed answers.

items.x: Not an acronym.
items.d: Static stability is the initial tendency of the airplane to return toward equilibrium after a disturbance. Positive static stability is an initial tendency to return to the original state, neutral static stability is a tendency to remain in the new condition, and negative static stability is a tendency to continue away from the original state. A forward center of gravity increases longitudinal static stability; an aft center of gravity reduces it.
items.reg: FAA-H-8083-25, Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, Chapter 5, Aerodynamics of Flight
items.why: Likely as the theory behind the weight and balance consequences he will ask about.

items.x: Not an acronym.
items.d: Dynamic stability describes the motion over time after a disturbance. Positive dynamic stability means the oscillation decreases in amplitude and the airplane returns to equilibrium, neutral dynamic stability means the amplitude neither grows nor decays, and negative dynamic stability means the motion diverges. An airplane can be statically stable but dynamically unstable, which is the distinction examiners test.
items.reg: FAA-H-8083-25, Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, Chapter 5, Aerodynamics of Flight
items.why: Always asked alongside static stability to see whether the applicant can separate the two.

items.x: Not an acronym.
items.d: In a coordinated turn the horizontal component of lift exactly balances the centrifugal force and the ball is centered. In a slipping turn the centrifugal force is less than the horizontal component of lift, so the airplane slips toward the inside of the turn and the ball falls to the inside. In a skidding turn the centrifugal force exceeds the horizontal component of lift, the airplane skids toward the outside, and the ball moves to the outside. A skidding turn at low airspeed on base to final is the classic stall and spin accident.
items.reg: FAA-H-8083-25, Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, Chapter 5, Aerodynamics of Flight; FAA-H-8083-3, Airplane Flying Handbook, Chapter 3
items.why: Likely as the risk management discussion attached to the maneuvers and the pattern.

items.x: Not an acronym. Named for Daniel Bernoulli.
items.d: Bernoulli's principle states that an increase in the speed of a fluid occurs simultaneously with a decrease in its pressure or potential energy. As air accelerates over the cambered upper surface of a wing it produces an area of lower pressure, while slower air beneath produces relatively higher pressure, and the difference contributes an upward force. Newton's third law, turning the airflow downward, is the complementary explanation and most examiners want both mentioned.
items.reg: FAA-H-8083-25, Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, Chapter 5, Aerodynamics of Flight
items.why: Possible as a warm-up theory question but rarely dwelt on at commercial level.

items.x: Not an acronym. Lift, weight, thrust and drag.
items.d: Lift opposes weight and thrust opposes drag, and in unaccelerated straight-and-level flight the opposing pairs are in equilibrium. The Gold Seal guide's diagram on page 13 labels the downward force Gravity rather than Weight; the standard FAA term is weight, which is the force of gravity acting on the mass of the airplane. Equilibrium does not mean the forces are equal in pairs at all times, only that the sums balance in unaccelerated flight.
items.reg: FAA-H-8083-25, Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, Chapter 5, Aerodynamics of Flight
items.why: Basic theory, possible as an opener but well below his systems focus.

items.t: Night, Civil Twilight and the Three Night Definitions
items.x: Not an acronym.
items.d: Night for logging purposes is the time between the end of evening civil twilight and the beginning of morning civil twilight, as published in the Air Almanac and converted to local time. Position lights must be on from sunset to sunrise. Night takeoff and landing currency for carrying passengers applies from 1 hour after sunset to 1 hour before sunrise. Civil twilight begins or ends when the geometric center of the sun is 6 degrees below the horizon, usually 20 to 35 minutes from sunset or sunrise.
items.reg: 14 CFR Part 1, Section 1.1, General definitions; 14 CFR Part 91, Subpart C, Section 91.209, Aircraft lights; 14 CFR Part 61, Subpart A, Section 61.57, Recent flight experience: Pilot in command, paragraph (b)
items.why: Three different definitions of night is a standard trap, and night carriage is a commercial privilege limitation.

items.x: Not an acronym.
items.d: No person may operate an aircraft from sunset to sunrise unless it has lighted position lights, nor may an aircraft be parked or moved in a night-operating area unless it is lighted or its lights are on. The Gold Seal guide states that anticollision lights are required from sunset to sunrise, which is incomplete: anticollision lights are required for all operations, day and night, on aircraft certificated with them, and the pilot in command may turn them off only when he determines that in the interest of safety it is better to do so.
items.reg: 14 CFR Part 91, Subpart C, Section 91.209, Aircraft lights
items.why: Likely on a night-carriage question, and the guide's version is wrong on anticollision lights.

items.x: Not an acronym. Commonly memorized as 3-152 and the 1-5-2 and 5-111 patterns.
items.d: Class B requires 3 statute miles and clear of clouds. Class C, Class D and Class E below 10,000 feet MSL require 3 statute miles with 500 feet below, 1,000 feet above and 2,000 feet horizontal. Class E at or above 10,000 feet MSL requires 5 statute miles with 1,000 feet below, 1,000 feet above and 1 statute mile horizontal. Class G at or below 1,200 feet AGL requires 1 statute mile and clear of clouds by day, 3 statute miles with the 500-1,000-2,000 clearances at night; above 1,200 feet AGL and below 10,000 feet MSL it is 1 statute mile by day and 3 at night with 500-1,000-2,000; above 1,200 feet AGL and at or above 10,000 feet MSL it is 5 statute miles with 1,000-1,000 and 1 statute mile.
items.reg: 14 CFR Part 91, Subpart B, Section 91.155, Basic VFR weather minimums
items.why: Memory-table recitation that most examiners spot-check rather than walk in full.

items.x: S - Special. V - Visual. F - Flight. R - Rules.
items.d: Special VFR is an ATC clearance to operate within the lateral boundaries of controlled airspace at an airport, below 10,000 feet MSL, clear of clouds with at least 1 statute mile flight visibility, when conditions are below basic VFR. Between sunset and sunrise the pilot must hold an instrument rating and the aircraft must be equipped for instrument flight. Some airports prohibit it, as marked on the sectional.
items.reg: 14 CFR Part 91, Subpart B, Section 91.157, Special VFR weather minimums
items.why: Listed on page 32 and the night restriction ties to the commercial instrument-rating limitation.

items.x: Not an acronym.
items.d: Steady green means cleared for takeoff on the ground and cleared to land in flight. Flashing green means cleared to taxi on the ground and return for landing in flight. Steady red means stop on the ground and give way to other aircraft and continue circling in flight. Flashing red means taxi clear of the landing area on the ground and airport unsafe, do not land, in flight. Flashing white means return to the starting point on the airport and is not used for aircraft in flight. Alternating red and green is a general warning signal to exercise extreme caution.
items.reg: 14 CFR Part 91, Subpart B, Section 91.125, ATC light signals; Aeronautical Information Manual, Paragraph 4-3-13, Traffic Control Light Signals
items.why: A table an examiner can quiz straight off the page, often triggered by an electrical failure scenario, which touches his focus.

items.x: Not an acronym.
items.d: To operate an aircraft not equipped with a transponder in Class B airspace, a request for deviation must be submitted to the controlling ATC facility at least 1 hour before the proposed operation. If the transponder fails in flight within Class B, an immediate request may obtain a deviation to allow the flight to continue. The same regulation also provides for deviations for the Mode C veil.
items.reg: 14 CFR Part 91, Subpart C, Section 91.215, ATC transponder and altitude reporting equipment and use
items.why: An electrical failure scenario in disguise, which is the kind of question his focus produces.

items.x: N - Notice. O - To. A - Air. M - Missions. Formerly Notice to Airmen.
items.d: A NOTAM is a notice of information essential to personnel concerned with flight operations that was not known far enough in advance to be publicized by other means. Types include flight data center NOTAMs for regulatory changes such as amended procedures, distant and local NOTAMs, and pointer NOTAMs. Checking NOTAMs is the N in NW KRAFT and is required by Section 91.103.
items.reg: 14 CFR Part 91, Subpart B, Section 91.103, Preflight action; Aeronautical Information Manual, Paragraph 5-1-3, Notice to Air Missions (NOTAM) System
items.why: Listed on page 31 and required by the preflight action regulation he will quote.

items.x: N - National. A - Airspace. S - System.
items.d: The national airspace system is the network of airspace, navigation facilities, airports, air traffic control facilities, rules, procedures and personnel that together support flight in the United States. The Gold Seal guide's page 15 diagram shows Class A from 18,000 feet MSL to flight level 600, Class B, C and D around airports, Class E as everywhere else including bases at 700 and 1,200 feet AGL, and Class G beneath.
items.reg: 14 CFR Part 71, Designation of Class A, B, C, D, and E Airspace Areas; Aeronautical Information Manual, Chapter 3, Airspace
items.why: Listed on page 31, and the airspace walk is standard even when the examiner's heart is in systems.

items.x: M - Military. O - Operations. A - Area.
items.d: A military operations area is airspace established to separate certain military training activities from IFR traffic. VFR aircraft may transit a MOA without a clearance, but should exercise extreme caution when it is active and should contact the controlling agency for traffic advisories. Activity times are published on the chart and in the chart supplement.
items.reg: Aeronautical Information Manual, Paragraph 3-4-5, Military Operations Areas
items.why: On the page 31 list and part of a routine special-use airspace sweep.

items.x: MTR: M - Military. T - Training. R - Route. IR: I - IFR. R - Route.
items.d: Military training routes are corridors used for military flight training at speeds above 250 knots. An IR is an IFR military training route and a VR is a VFR military training route. Routes with four-digit numbers operate entirely at or below 1,500 feet AGL, and routes with three-digit numbers include segments above 1,500 feet AGL.
items.reg: Aeronautical Information Manual, Paragraph 3-5-2, Military Training Routes
items.why: Page 31 and 32 vocabulary, possible in a chart review but unlikely to be dwelt on.

items.x: M - Maximum. E - Elevation. F - Figure.
items.d: The maximum elevation figure is the number printed in each quadrangle on a sectional chart showing the highest known feature in that quadrangle, including terrain and obstructions, in thousands and hundreds of feet MSL. It is a charting convention used for terrain avoidance planning, not a minimum safe altitude.
items.reg: FAA Aeronautical Chart User's Guide; Aeronautical Information Manual, Chapter 9, Aeronautical Charts and Related Publications
items.why: On the page 31 list and possible during a cross-country chart review.

items.x: N - Near. M - Midair. A - Collision.
items.d: A near midair collision is an incident in which the possibility of collision occurs as a result of proximity of less than 500 feet between aircraft, or a report from a pilot or crewmember that a collision hazard existed. Pilots are urged to report them to the nearest FAA facility.
items.reg: Aeronautical Information Manual, Paragraph 7-7-3, Near Midair Collision Reporting
items.why: Page 31 vocabulary with no practical question attached on a commercial ride.

items.x: Not an acronym.
items.d: The prohibition on portable electronic devices applies to aircraft operated by an air carrier or commercial operator, or to any aircraft operated under IFR; it does not blanket all Part 91 VFR flying, which the Gold Seal guide's page 10 summary does not make clear. The exceptions are portable voice recorders, hearing aids, heart pacemakers, electric shavers and any other device the operator has determined will not interfere with navigation or communication systems.
items.reg: 14 CFR Part 91, Subpart A, Section 91.21, Portable electronic devices
items.why: Included for completeness; it almost never comes up and the guide's framing is too broad.

items.x: Not an acronym.
items.d: To carry passengers you must have made 3 takeoffs and 3 landings within the preceding 90 days as sole manipulator of the controls in an aircraft of the same category, class and, if a type rating is required, type. In a tailwheel airplane the landings must be to a full stop. For passengers at night, between 1 hour after sunset and 1 hour before sunrise, the 3 takeoffs and landings must be to a full stop within the preceding 90 days.
items.reg: 14 CFR Part 61, Subpart A, Section 61.57, Recent flight experience: Pilot in command, paragraphs (a) and (b)
items.why: A commercial pilot carries passengers for a living, so the currency rule is a near-certain question.

items.x: Not an acronym.
items.d: The commercial single-engine airplane applicant needs 250 hours total time, including at least 100 hours in powered aircraft of which 50 are in airplanes, 100 hours pilot in command of which 50 are in airplanes and 50 are cross-country with 10 in airplanes, 20 hours of training in the Section 61.127(b)(1) areas of operation including 10 hours of instrument training, 10 hours in a complex or technically advanced airplane, and 3 hours of test preparation within the preceding 2 calendar months. The cross-country requirements include one flight of at least 300 nautical miles total with landings at a minimum of three points one of which is at least 250 nautical miles straight-line from the original departure point, a 2-hour day cross-country of more than 100 nautical miles straight-line distance, and a 2-hour night cross-country of more than 100 nautical miles. Night requires 5 hours in night VFR conditions with 10 takeoffs and 10 landings in the traffic pattern at an airport with an operating control tower.
items.reg: 14 CFR Part 61, Subpart F, Section 61.129, Aeronautical experience
items.why: He will verify the logbook against this list before the oral, but it is paperwork rather than knowledge.

items.x: Not an acronym.
items.d: To be eligible for a commercial pilot certificate you must be at least 18 years of age, be able to read, speak, write and understand English, receive and log the required ground and flight training with the required endorsements, pass the knowledge test on the Section 61.125 areas, pass the practical test on the Section 61.127 areas of operation, meet the Section 61.129 aeronautical experience requirements, and hold at least a private pilot certificate or meet the Section 61.73 requirements. An instrument rating alone does not satisfy the commercial training requirements.
items.reg: 14 CFR Part 61, Subpart F, Section 61.123, Eligibility requirements: General
items.why: Verified at the paperwork stage, so it is checked but not usually discussed.

items.x: Not an acronym.
items.d: No person may act as pilot in command unless, within the preceding 24 calendar months, he has accomplished a flight review consisting of at least 1 hour of flight training and 1 hour of ground training with an authorized instructor and received a logbook endorsement. It may be satisfied instead by a proficiency check, a practical test for a new certificate or rating, or completion of one or more phases of the FAA WINGS pilot proficiency program. Passing this commercial practical test satisfies the flight review.
items.reg: 14 CFR Part 61, Subpart A, Section 61.56, Flight review
items.why: Likely as a currency sweep, and the fact that the checkride itself resets it is a nice answer.

items.x: Not an acronym.
items.d: A complex airplane endorsement is required for an airplane with retractable landing gear, flaps and a controllable pitch propeller. A high-performance endorsement is required for an airplane with an engine of more than 200 horsepower. A high-altitude endorsement is required for a pressurized airplane with a service ceiling or maximum operating altitude, whichever is lower, above 25,000 feet MSL. A tailwheel endorsement is required for a tailwheel airplane and covers normal and crosswind takeoffs and landings, wheel landings and go-around procedures. None of these specify a minimum number of hours; all require ground and flight training and a logbook endorsement.
items.reg: 14 CFR Part 61, Subpart A, Section 61.31, Type rating requirements, additional training, and authorization requirements
items.why: Likely because the Warrior is neither complex nor high-performance, which invites the question of what he trained in.

items.x: T - Technically. A - Advanced. A - Airplane.
items.d: A technically advanced airplane is one with an electronically advanced avionics system including a primary flight display, a multifunction display with moving map and navigation, and a two-axis autopilot integrated with navigation and heading guidance. Ten hours in a complex airplane, a turbine-powered airplane or a technically advanced airplane satisfies the Section 61.129 training requirement for the single-engine commercial certificate.
items.reg: 14 CFR Part 61, Subpart F, Section 61.129, Aeronautical experience, paragraph (j)
items.why: It is how most applicants now satisfy the complex requirement, so he will ask which path was used.

items.x: 6 - Six instrument approaches. H - Holding procedures and tasks. I - Intercepting courses. T - Tracking courses. S - Using navigational electronic systems.
items.d: Instrument currency requires that within the preceding 6 calendar months the pilot has performed and logged six instrument approaches, holding procedures and tasks, and intercepting and tracking courses using navigational electronic systems, in the appropriate category of aircraft or an approved simulator, flight training device or aviation training device. If currency lapses there is a further 6 months of grace in which it can be regained with a safety pilot or instructor, after which an instrument proficiency check is required.
items.reg: 14 CFR Part 61, Subpart A, Section 61.57, Recent flight experience: Pilot in command, paragraph (c)
items.why: This is a single-engine land commercial ride under Part 91, so instrument currency is background rather than a test subject.

items.x: I - Instrument. P - Proficiency. C - Check.
items.d: An instrument proficiency check is required to regain instrument privileges once more than 12 calendar months have passed since currency lapsed, and it must be administered by an examiner, an authorized instructor with an instrument rating, or an FAA-approved person. Some tasks may be conducted in an approved aviation training device.
items.reg: 14 CFR Part 61, Subpart A, Section 61.57, Recent flight experience: Pilot in command, paragraph (d)
items.why: Instrument housekeeping, outside the scope of a commercial single-engine land ride.

items.x: Not an acronym.
items.d: When a pilot operates in simulated instrument flight in an airplane, a safety pilot must occupy the other control seat. The safety pilot must hold at least a private pilot certificate with category and class ratings appropriate to the aircraft, hold a current medical certificate, and the aircraft must have dual controls and adequate forward and side vision for both pilots. The Gold Seal guide correctly notes the safety pilot need not be current.
items.reg: 14 CFR Part 91, Subpart B, Section 91.109, Flight instruction; Simulated instrument flight and certain flight tests; 14 CFR Part 61, Subpart A, Section 61.3, Requirement for certificates, ratings, and authorizations
items.why: Possible as a logging question but not a commercial single-engine focus area.

items.x: Not an acronym.
items.d: A person may log instrument time only for that flight time when the aircraft is operated solely by reference to instruments under actual or simulated instrument conditions, and an authorized instructor may log instrument time when conducting instrument flight instruction in actual instrument conditions. Each instrument approach logged must record the location and type of approach, the safety pilot's name if one was required, and the simulator or training device used.
items.reg: 14 CFR Part 61, Subpart A, Section 61.51, Pilot logbooks, paragraph (g)
items.why: Logbook mechanics he may spot-check while reviewing the records.

items.x: C - Certificated. F - Flight. I - Instructor.
items.d: A certificated flight instructor holds a flight instructor certificate under Part 61 Subpart H and may give the training and endorsements required for certificates and ratings. Many commercial pilots go on to add the instructor certificate, and instruction given for hire in an aircraft the instructor provides is one of the Section 119.1 paragraph (e) operations.
items.reg: 14 CFR Part 61, Subpart H, Flight Instructors Other Than Flight Instructors With a Sport Pilot Rating; 14 CFR Part 119, Subpart A, Section 119.1, Applicability, paragraph (e)
items.why: Page 31 vocabulary, relevant mainly as a career follow-up to the commercial certificate.

items.x: Not a letter-by-letter acronym. WINGS is the name of the FAA Pilot Proficiency Program.
items.d: The WINGS program is a phased FAA-sponsored proficiency award program, and completing one or more phases substitutes for the Section 61.56 flight review. It is listed in the Gold Seal guide as one of the flight review substitutions.
items.reg: 14 CFR Part 61, Subpart A, Section 61.56, Flight review; Advisory Circular 61-91, WINGS - Pilot Proficiency Program
items.why: A footnote in the flight review answer, almost never asked directly.

items.x: D - Deviation. V - Variation. M - Magnetic dip. O - Oscillation. N - North and south turning errors. A - Acceleration errors.
items.d: DV MONA is the list of magnetic compass errors. Deviation is caused by magnetic fields within the airplane and is corrected by the compass correction card. Variation is the angular difference between true and magnetic north. Magnetic dip is the vertical pull of the earth's field near the poles, which causes the turning and acceleration errors. Oscillation is erratic swinging in turbulence.
items.reg: FAA-H-8083-25, Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, Chapter 8, Flight Instruments
items.why: A fixed list that examiners like, and a compass is required equipment under Section 91.205.

items.x: U - Undershoot. N - North. O - Overshoot. S - South.
items.d: UNOS describes the northerly turning error of the magnetic compass: when turning to a northerly heading the compass lags and you must undershoot the target heading, and when turning to a southerly heading it leads and you must overshoot. The error is greatest at north and south and is nil at east and west. The Gold Seal guide prints it on page 5 alongside DV MONA.
items.reg: FAA-H-8083-25, Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, Chapter 8, Flight Instruments
items.why: Short, memorizable and the kind of thing an examiner asks right after naming the compass errors.

items.x: A - Accelerate. N - North. D - Decelerate. S - South.
items.d: ANDS describes the acceleration error of the magnetic compass on east or west headings: accelerating produces an apparent turn to the north and decelerating produces an apparent turn to the south. Like the turning error it is caused by magnetic dip and it does not occur on north or south headings.
items.reg: FAA-H-8083-25, Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, Chapter 8, Flight Instruments
items.why: Paired with UNOS in the same breath, and it is the partial-panel follow-up.

items.x: Not an acronym.
items.d: No person may operate an aircraft under IFR using VOR unless the VOR has been operationally checked within the preceding 30 days. Permitted checks and tolerances are a VOT at plus or minus 4 degrees, a repair station signal at plus or minus 4 degrees, a designated ground checkpoint at plus or minus 4 degrees, a designated airborne checkpoint at plus or minus 6 degrees, a dual VOR cross-check at 4 degrees between the two, and an airborne check over a prominent ground landmark on a selected radial at least 20 nautical miles from the VOR at plus or minus 6 degrees. The date, place, bearing error and signature must be recorded.
items.reg: 14 CFR Part 91, Subpart B, Section 91.171, VOR equipment check for IFR operations
items.why: It is the V in AV1ATES, so he will reach it from the inspections mnemonic even on a VFR ride.

items.x: Not an acronym.
items.d: No person may operate an aircraft in IFR conditions unless it carries enough fuel to complete the flight to the first airport of intended landing, then fly from that airport to the alternate if one is required, and then fly after that for 45 minutes at normal cruising speed. Under VFR the reserve is 30 minutes by day and 45 minutes at night at normal cruising speed.
items.reg: 14 CFR Part 91, Subpart B, Section 91.167, Fuel requirements for flight in IFR conditions; 14 CFR Part 91, Subpart B, Section 91.151, Fuel requirements for flight in VFR conditions
items.why: Fuel planning is a named focus area even though the IFR half is secondary on this ride.

items.x: V - Very high frequency. O - Omnidirectional. R - Range.
items.d: A VHF omnidirectional range is a ground-based navigation aid transmitting radials outward in all directions, read in the cockpit on a course deviation indicator with an omnibearing selector. VOR signals are line of sight and are unaffected by the aircraft's heading, which is why the indication depends only on position relative to the selected radial. A VORTAC is a colocated VOR and TACAN, and a VOT is a VOR test facility.
items.reg: Aeronautical Information Manual, Paragraph 1-1-3, VHF Omni-directional Range (VOR); 14 CFR Part 91, Subpart B, Section 91.171, VOR equipment check for IFR operations
items.why: Page 32 vocabulary, usually only touched during the cross-country planning discussion.

items.x: CDI: C - Course. D - Deviation. I - Indicator. OBS: O - Omnibearing. B - Selector, the omnibearing selector.
items.d: The course deviation indicator is the needle that shows displacement left or right of the selected course, and the omnibearing selector is the knob and card used to select that course. On a VOR each dot of CDI deflection is normally 2 degrees, with full-scale deflection at 10 degrees. On an ILS the CDI is roughly four times as sensitive.
items.reg: Aeronautical Information Manual, Paragraph 1-1-3, VHF Omni-directional Range (VOR)
items.why: Page 31 and 32 vocabulary, incidental on a VFR commercial ride.

items.x: RNAV: R - aRea. NAV - Navigation. WAAS: W - Wide. A - Area. A - Augmentation. S - System.
items.d: Area navigation permits navigation on any desired path within the coverage of ground or space-based navigation aids, rather than directly to and from stations. The wide area augmentation system corrects GPS signals to allow vertically guided approaches. The alternate planning rule in the Gold Seal guide notes that without WAAS you may plan for RNAV approaches at either the destination or the alternate but not both, and with WAAS you may plan for RNAV at both.
items.reg: 14 CFR Part 91, Subpart B, Section 91.169, IFR flight plan: Information required; Aeronautical Information Manual, Paragraph 1-1-17, Global Positioning System (GPS)
items.why: Page 32 vocabulary with an IFR planning rule attached, which is secondary on this ride.

items.x: Not an acronym. Commonly memorized as MARVELOUS VFR C500.
items.d: Reports to ATC without request include leaving a final approach fix inbound, a missed approach, any unforecast weather, any safety-of-flight information, vacating a previously assigned altitude or flight level, reaching a holding fix with time and altitude, leaving an assigned holding fix, an inability to climb or descend at least 500 feet per minute, loss of navigation or communication capability, and a change in average true airspeed at cruise of 5 percent or 10 knots from that filed. When not in radar contact, also report compulsory reporting points and the time and altitude reaching a holding fix or clearance limit.
items.reg: 14 CFR Part 91, Subpart B, Section 91.183, IFR communications; Aeronautical Information Manual, Paragraph 5-3-3, Additional Reports
items.why: On pages 3 of the guide but it belongs to the instrument rating, not a single-engine land commercial ride.

items.x: HSI: H - Horizontal. S - Situation. I - Indicator. RMI: R - Radio. M - Magnetic. I - Indicator.
items.d: A horizontal situation indicator combines the heading indicator and the course deviation indicator into one display, so course deviation is always shown relative to the airplane's actual heading. A radio magnetic indicator combines a rotating compass card with one or more bearing pointers that always point to the station. Both reduce the mental rotation required for orientation.
items.reg: FAA-H-8083-15, Instrument Flying Handbook, Chapter 5, Flight Instruments
items.why: Page 31 and 32 vocabulary with no bearing on a VFR single-engine commercial ride.

items.x: RB: R - Relative. B - Bearing. MB: M - Magnetic. B - Bearing. MH: M - Magnetic. H - Heading.
items.d: Relative bearing is the angle from the nose of the aircraft clockwise to the station. Magnetic bearing is the angle from magnetic north to the station. Magnetic heading is the direction the nose points relative to magnetic north. The relationship is magnetic heading plus relative bearing equals magnetic bearing, correcting by 360 degrees as needed, which is the classic ADF problem.
items.reg: FAA-H-8083-15, Instrument Flying Handbook, Chapter 9, Navigation Systems
items.why: Page 31 and 32 vocabulary from an era of ADF navigation, included for completeness.

items.x: ILS: I - Instrument. L - Landing. S - System. IAP: I - Instrument. A - Approach. P - Procedure.
items.d: An instrument landing system is a precision approach aid providing lateral guidance from a localizer and vertical guidance from a glideslope. An instrument approach procedure is the published series of predetermined maneuvers for the orderly transfer of an aircraft under instrument conditions from the beginning of the initial approach to a landing or to a point from which a visual landing may be made. The availability of at least one instrument approach is the first test in the Section 91.169 alternate decision.
items.reg: 14 CFR Part 91, Subpart B, Section 91.169, IFR flight plan: Information required; 14 CFR Part 97, Standard Instrument Procedures
items.why: Page 31 vocabulary that belongs to the instrument rating, not to this ride.

items.x: TACAN: T - Tactical. A - Air. N - Navigation. VORTAC is a colocated VOR and TACAN. VOT: V - VOR. O and T - test facility.
items.d: TACAN is the military ultra high frequency navigation system that provides bearing and distance, and a VORTAC is a facility where a civilian VOR and a military TACAN are colocated so that civil aircraft obtain VOR azimuth and DME distance from the TACAN component. A VOT is a VOR test facility that transmits a signal allowing a ground check of the VOR receiver with a tolerance of plus or minus 4 degrees.
items.reg: Aeronautical Information Manual, Paragraph 1-1-5, Tactical Air Navigation (TACAN); 14 CFR Part 91, Subpart B, Section 91.171, VOR equipment check for IFR operations
items.why: Page 32 vocabulary, reachable only through the VOR check item.

groups.g: General Abbreviations from the Guide's Terms and Definitions List

items.x: AGL: A - Above. G - Ground. L - Level. MSL: M - Mean. S - Sea. L - Level.
items.d: Above ground level is height measured from the terrain directly beneath the aircraft, and mean sea level is altitude measured from the average level of the sea. Airspace floors and ceilings, cloud clearances, and the commercial maneuver minimum of 1,500 feet AGL mix the two, so you must be precise about which is meant. Charted airport and obstacle elevations are MSL; obstacle heights in parentheses are AGL.
items.reg: 14 CFR Part 91, Subpart B, Section 91.119, Minimum safe altitudes: General; 14 CFR Part 91, Subpart B, Section 91.155, Basic VFR weather minimums
items.why: On the page 31 list and mixing them up is the single most common applicant error.

items.x: A - Advisory. C - Circular.
items.d: An advisory circular is FAA guidance material that explains an acceptable means, but not the only means, of complying with a regulation. Advisory circulars are not regulatory unless incorporated by reference into a rule. AC 120-12A on common versus private carriage and AC 61-142 on expense sharing are the two most relevant to commercial privileges.
items.reg: Advisory Circular 00-2, Advisory Circular Checklist
items.why: He will ask whether an advisory circular is binding, which is the standard trap.

items.x: A - Aeronautical. I - Information. M - Manual.
items.d: The Aeronautical Information Manual is the FAA's official guide to basic flight information and air traffic control procedures. It is not regulatory, but it describes the procedures pilots are expected to follow and it is the source for light gun signals, illusions, wake turbulence and weather advisory definitions. Several Gold Seal guide boxes cite AIM paragraphs rather than regulations, which is the right distinction to draw.
items.reg: Aeronautical Information Manual
items.why: He may ask whether a procedure you cite is regulatory or AIM guidance.

items.x: PHAK: P - Pilot's. H - Handbook of. A - Aeronautical. K - Knowledge. AFH: A - Airplane. F - Flying. H - Handbook. IFH: I - Instrument. F - Flying. H - Handbook. ACL: A - Aeronautical. C - Chart. L - Legend.
items.d: These are the FAA handbooks and references the ACS lists as source material. The Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge is FAA-H-8083-25, the Airplane Flying Handbook is FAA-H-8083-3 and the Instrument Flying Handbook is FAA-H-8083-15. The aeronautical chart legend, now the Chart User's Guide, explains sectional symbology. Knowing which book answers which question is a credible way to handle an item you do not know.
items.reg: FAA-S-ACS-7, Commercial Pilot for Airplane Category Airman Certification Standards, References
items.why: Naming the right source when you are unsure is a technique that keeps an oral moving.

items.x: A - Airport. F - Facility. D - Directory. The guide prints Airport/Facility Director, which is a typographical error.
items.d: The Airport Facility Directory was the regional booklet of airport data, communications frequencies, services and special notices. Two corrections to the Gold Seal guide entry: the final word is Directory, not Director, and the publication has been renamed the Chart Supplement, which is what you will actually be asked to produce for the cross-country planning portion.
items.reg: Aeronautical Information Manual, Paragraph 9-1-4, General Description of each Chart Series; 14 CFR Part 91, Subpart B, Section 91.103, Preflight action
items.why: He will ask for the Chart Supplement by its current name during the planning discussion, and the guide's entry is wrong twice over.

items.x: A - Air. T - Traffic. C - Control.
items.d: Air traffic control is the service operated to promote the safe, orderly and expeditious flow of air traffic. Under Part 91 the pilot in command remains the final authority and may deviate from an ATC clearance in an emergency, with a written report on request if a deviation from a rule was involved.
items.reg: 14 CFR Part 91, Subpart A, Section 91.3, Responsibility and authority of the pilot in command; 14 CFR Part 91, Subpart B, Section 91.123, Compliance with ATC clearances and instructions
items.why: Page 31 vocabulary, but the authority-versus-clearance question behind it is commonly asked.

items.x: N - National. T - Transportation. S - Safety. B - Board.
items.d: The National Transportation Safety Board investigates civil aviation accidents and is the body to which accidents and certain incidents must be reported under 49 CFR Part 830. Immediate notification is required for an accident and for listed serious incidents such as flight control system malfunction, in-flight fire, or complete loss of electrical power or inability of a required flight crewmember to perform duties. A report must be filed within 10 days of an accident.
items.reg: 49 CFR Part 830, Notification and Reporting of Aircraft Accidents or Incidents and Overdue Aircraft, and Preservation of Aircraft Wreckage, Mail, Cargo, and Records
items.why: Listed on page 31, and the immediate-notification list includes an electrical failure item that sits in his focus area.

items.x: U - Universal. T - Time. C - Coordinated. Written as Coordinated Universal Time and spoken as Zulu.
items.d: Coordinated Universal Time is the time standard used for all aviation weather reports, forecasts, flight plans and NOTAMs, so that no conversion errors occur across time zones. METARs and TAFs carry it with a trailing Z. You must be able to convert local time to Zulu both ways without hesitation.
items.reg: Aeronautical Information Manual, Paragraph 7-1-29, Key to Aviation Routine Weather Report (METAR) and Aerodrome Forecasts (TAF)
items.why: He will hand over a METAR and ask what time it was issued in local terms.

items.x: VFR: V - Visual. F - Flight. R - Rules. IFR: I - Instrument. F - Flight. R - Rules.
items.d: Visual flight rules govern flight conducted by outside visual reference, subject to the Section 91.155 visibility and cloud clearance minimums. Instrument flight rules govern flight conducted by reference to instruments under an ATC clearance. An instrument rating is required to act as pilot in command under IFR, in Class A airspace, for Special VFR at night, and for carrying passengers for compensation or hire on cross-countries over 50 nautical miles or at night.
items.reg: 14 CFR Part 91, Subpart B, Section 91.155, Basic VFR weather minimums; 14 CFR Part 61, Subpart A, Section 61.3, Requirement for certificates, ratings, and authorizations; 14 CFR Part 61, Subpart F, Section 61.133, Commercial pilot privileges and limitations
items.why: Page 31 and 32 vocabulary, but the list of when an instrument rating is required is a real commercial question.

items.x: FAA: F - Federal. A - Aviation. A - Administration. FAR: F - Federal. A - Aviation. R - Regulation.
items.d: The Federal Aviation Administration is the agency that regulates civil aviation in the United States. The regulations are properly cited as Title 14 of the Code of Federal Regulations, 14 CFR, and the older label FAR is ambiguous because it also denotes the Federal Acquisition Regulation. Cite part, subpart and section by number and title on the oral.
items.reg: Title 14, Code of Federal Regulations, Aeronautics and Space
items.why: On the page 31 list; good practice for citing cleanly, but not a question in itself.

items.x: FSS: F - Flight. S - Service. S - Station. FSDO: F - Flight. S - Standards. D - District. O - Office.
items.d: A flight service station provides preflight briefings, flight plan filing, en route advisories and search and rescue initiation. A Flight Standards District Office is the local FAA field office responsible for certification, surveillance and enforcement, and it is where you go for a special flight permit or a certificate replacement. They are easy to confuse and serve entirely different functions.
items.reg: Aeronautical Information Manual, Paragraph 4-1-3, Flight Service Stations; 14 CFR Part 21, Subpart H, Section 21.197, Special flight permits
items.why: Page 31 vocabulary, reached mainly through the special flight permit answer.

items.x: E - Estimated. T - Time. E - En route.
items.d: Estimated time en route is the planned flight time between departure and destination, computed from groundspeed and distance, and it is a required element of a flight plan. It feeds directly into the fuel reserve calculation and into the Section 91.169 alternate window of 1 hour before to 1 hour after the estimated time of arrival.
items.reg: 14 CFR Part 91, Subpart B, Section 91.153, VFR flight plan: Information required; 14 CFR Part 91, Subpart B, Section 91.169, IFR flight plan: Information required
items.why: Page 31 vocabulary, used in passing during the cross-country planning.

items.x: FL - Flight. Comp - Computer.
items.d: The flight computer is the mechanical E6B or electronic equivalent used to compute wind correction angle, groundspeed, time, fuel burn, density altitude and true airspeed. An examiner may hand you one and ask you to solve a wind triangle or a density altitude problem without an application.
items.reg: FAA-H-8083-25, Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, Chapter 16, Navigation
items.why: Page 31 vocabulary, but he may insist on a manual computation during the planning portion.

items.x: SFC: Surface. SL: S - Sea. L - Level. ST: S - Standard. T - Temperature.
items.d: Surface denotes ground level, used for airspace floors described as surface to a stated altitude and for the surface visibility remark in a METAR. Sea level is the reference datum for MSL altitudes and for standard pressure. Standard temperature is 15 degrees Celsius at sea level, decreasing approximately 2 degrees Celsius per 1,000 feet, and it is the baseline against which density altitude is computed.
items.reg: FAA-H-8083-25, Pilot's Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, Chapter 11, Aircraft Performance
items.why: Page 31 and 32 vocabulary; the standard temperature value itself does get asked.

items.x: V - Very. H - High. F - Frequency.
items.d: The very high frequency band, from 30 to 300 megahertz, carries aviation voice communications from 118.000 to 136.975 megahertz and VOR navigation from 108.00 to 117.95 megahertz. VHF is line of sight, so reception range increases with altitude, which is the practical point behind a radio failure at low altitude.
items.reg: Aeronautical Information Manual, Paragraph 4-2-1, General, Radio Communications Phraseology and Techniques
items.why: Page 32 vocabulary, reached only through a communications failure scenario.

items.x: F - Fixed. B - Base. O - Operator. The guide prints Fixed-Based Operator.
items.d: A fixed base operator is a business at an airport providing fuel, maintenance, hangarage, flight training or charter. The usual spelling is fixed base operator rather than the guide's fixed-based operator. For a commercial pilot the FBO is often the employer, which makes the carriage and operational control questions practical rather than theoretical.
items.why: Page 31 vocabulary with no question attached.

items.x: D - Direct. U - User. A - Access. T - Terminal. S - Service. The guide omits the final S.
items.d: The Direct User Access Terminal Service was a government-funded online weather briefing and flight plan filing system. It was discontinued in 2018 and replaced by commercial providers and by the FAA's own online briefing service. The Gold Seal guide lists it on page 31 as Direct User Access Terminal, missing the Service, and does not note that it no longer exists.
items.reg: Aeronautical Information Manual, Paragraph 7-1-2, FAA Weather Services
items.why: A retired service on the page 31 list, included only for completeness.

items.x: AAF: A - Army. A - Air. F - Field. AFB: A - Air. F - Force. B - Base.
items.d: Army airfield and air force base are military airport designations appearing in airport names and on charts. They matter chiefly because military fields carry their own operating requirements and prior permission rules, which are published in the Chart Supplement.
items.reg: Aeronautical Information Manual, Paragraph 4-1-5, Pilot Visits to Air Traffic Facilities
items.why: Pure page 31 chart vocabulary with no question behind it.
